During sleep and quiet wakefulness, the brain spontaneously revisits neural activity patterns associated with previous experience, a phenomenon known as reactivation, or replay. Reactivation is thought to support systems consolidation, the process by which memory retrieval becomes progressively more dependent on neocortical circuits and less dependent on the hippocampus. Importantly, reactivation is not indiscriminate: it preferentially targets specific memories, such as new or weakly learned ones.
These observations have motivated the development of computational models accounting for the spontaneous reactivation of memories, their prioritisation for replay, and their transfer between the hippocampus and neocortex. In parallel, predictive-coding (PC) models have shown how computations attributed to hippocampal and neocortical circuits can arise from local prediction-error dynamics. Here, we connect these two lines of work by showing how autonomous intrinsic dynamics in coupled PC networks can transfer stored memory content between neural systems.
The hippocampus and neocortex are modelled as two coupled PC associative memory networks, with asymmetric coupling motivated by reported interactions between hippocampal area CA1 and the prefrontal cortex. This coupling establishes a closed-loop dialogue in which hippocampal activity drives neocortical learning, while neocortical feedback biases subsequent hippocampal activity toward content for which neocortical support remains weak. We prove that this feedback steers hippocampal activity toward states of higher neocortical free energy, so that prioritisation emerges from the dynamics rather than from an explicit scheduler.
In our model, neocortical learning relies exclusively on spontaneous hippocampal activity, without access to the initial training corpus. Nevertheless, we show that the neocortical network acquires correlated memory content faster than direct training on randomly sampled memories. This advantage appeared for sufficiently correlated memories, grew with their correlation, and persisted when new memories were incrementally added during transfer.
Together, these results provide a PC account in which neocortical feedback organises hippocampal reactivation to support efficient memory transfer during systems consolidation.

Article.Title: Thalamocortical credit routing from the basal ganglia and cerebellum: anatomical constraints and circuit principles
Article.Authors: Tanno, S.; Morishima, M.; Fujita, K.; Kato, S.; Kobayashi, K.; Kawaguchi, Y.; Isomura, Y.; Hira, R.
Article.Abstract: Animals learn to select actions that maximize reward in complex environments. A central challenge in this process is credit routing: behavioral outcomes must be routed back to the neural populations that contributed to generating the relevant actions. One possible route is through thalamocortical pathways conveying learning signals from the basal ganglia and cerebellum, where plasticity is shaped by reward-prediction errors. However, how these pathways route such signals back to specific cortical circuits remains unclear. To address this question, we combined anatomical circuit mapping in mice with closed-loop circuit modeling. Anterograde transsynaptic tracing revealed that thalamic neurons receiving input from the substantia nigra pars reticulata or the lateral cerebellar nucleus were largely segregated, with partial overlap in the ventromedial thalamus. Nevertheless, their cortical axons shared a pronounced enrichment in layer 1a, most prominently in secondary motor cortex. In a brain- wide synergistic loop-circuit model, learning was enhanced when both pathways delivered additive and gain-modulating feedback aligned with the cortical action readout. Local activity- based calibration established this alignment, whereas dendritic-spike- and reward-prediction- error-dependent thalamocortical plasticity further refined behavioral output. Module-specific feedback was essential for a brain-machine interface task requiring the simultaneous conditioning of multiple target neurons. Together, these findings define a credit-routing architecture in which laminar convergence, plastic alignment, and modular feedback link parallel subcortical learning systems to cortical action representations.

Article.Title: Auditory and visual mismatch negativity responses to numerical and non-numerical magnitudes in adults
Article.Authors: Mobeen, S.; Koponen, T.; Torppa, M.; Hämäläinen, J.; Lohvansuu, K.
Article.Abstract:
We investigated how auditory and visual presentation of small numerical magnitudes and non- numerical magnitudes are passively processed at the neural level. Earlier research suggests automatic processing of quantities occurs rapidly in the brain. However, there are no studies on passive, pre-attentive change detection of magnitudes utilizing mismatch negativity (MMN) across sensory modalities in same participants, important to understand amodal processing of magnitudes. We recorded EEG in passive auditory and visual multi-feature oddball and control paradigms from the same adult individuals (N=104/105, respectively). In the auditory paradigm, the standard stimulus was a 2-part sound, while the deviant stimuli varied in frequency, intensity, gap length, and number of sounds (1-part and 3-part stimuli). In the visual paradigm, the standard stimulus was a dot array containing two medium-sized dots, while the deviant stimuli varied in numerosity (1 or 3 dots) and dot size (small or large).
The results for the auditory paradigm showed significant MMN across all features, including comparisons with deviant-alone control stimuli, except for the 2-part vs. 1-part contrast. The results for the visual paradigm suggested differences in processing across all features apart from large and medium-size stimuli. These results replicate earlier MMN findings that the brain distinguishes pre-attentively changes in sound frequency, amplitude and gap. Auditorily presented small numerical magnitudes also showed pre-attentive processing but less robustly to the contrast 2 vs. 1. Visual pre-attentive processing of small numerical magnitudes was also observed. Together these findings could be interpreted to support the existence of abstract, pre- attentive processing of numerical magnitudes.
Highlights* Auditory and visual processing of numerical and non-numerical magnitudes was examined with EEG
* Auditory non-numerical magnitudes and medium vs. small dots replicated earlier MMN studies
* aMMN and vMMN showed pre-attentive processing of changes in small numerosities 2 vs. 3 and 2 vs. 1
* 2 vs. 1 tone processing was less robust than 2 vs. 3 or the processing of the visual contrasts
* The brain processes changes in small non-symbolic magnitudes pre-attentively

Article.Title: RADIAL AND TANGENTIAL FIBER COMPONENTS IN HUMAN SUPERFICIAL WHITE MATTER AND THEIR ASSOCIATIONS WITH MACROSCALE FUNCTION
Article.Authors: Hwang, Y.; Vavassori, L.; Bautin, P.; Rodriguez-Cruces, R.; Gaspar-Martinez, E.; Cabalo, D. G.; Ngo, A.; Smith, M.; Leech, R.; Coronado-Leija, R.; Petit, L.; Avesani, P.; Sarubbo, S.; Evans, A. C.; Concha, L.; Bernhardt, B. C.
Article.Abstract:
The superficial white matter (SWM), a thin layer of white matter beneath the cortex, contains a complex arrangement of short- and long-range fiber systems that support communication between cortical regions. These fiber populations include subcortical U-shaped fibers (U-fibers) that predominantly follow a tangential trajectory along the gray matter-white matter interface and long-range fibers that extend more radially through the deeper white matter to connect distant cortical regions. Here, we developed a surface-based framework to dissociate radial and tangential fiber components within the human SWM and investigated their microstructural properties and functional relevance using in-vivo high-field MRI. These components were quantified using apparent fiber density (AFD), fractional anisotropy (FA), and mean diffusivity (MD). We further contextualized SWM fiber architecture by examining depth-dependent microstructural profiles and their relationship with normative patterns of cortical organization and hierarchical specialization. The anatomical assessment of the proposed fiber orientation separation was supported by tractography-based bundle analyses, while the anatomical accuracy of tractography reconstructions was confirmed through comparison with post-mortem white matter dissection data. To assess their functional relevance, the fiber predominance map derived from radial and tangential AFD was related to spatial patterns of functional variability across the cortex. Regions with greater radially oriented fiber contribution exhibited more gradual changes in functional similarity across geodesic distance, whereas tangentially oriented fiber-enriched regions showed more rapid local functional differentiation. These findings reveal distinct structural and functional signatures of radial and tangential SWM fiber components and provide a framework for investigating their contributions to cortical organization and functional specialization.
SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENTThe human cerebral cortex is organized into specialized regions that support diverse functions, but the structural principles underlying this organization remain incompletely understood. The superficial white matter (SWM), a thin layer of white matter beneath the cortex, contains intermingled short- and long-range fiber systems that support communication between cortical regions. However, these fiber populations have remained difficult to characterize because they are closely intertwined within the SWM. By developing a reproducible framework for mapping and quantifying distinct SWM fiber systems, this work provides a foundation for systematic investigation of this complex compartment. Integration of multimodal datasets, together with open sharing of analytical tools and standardized features, promotes transparency, reproducibility, enabling future studies of how superficial connectivity supports brain organization.

Article.Title: Impaired value estimation over space explains turn-induced freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease: A cortico-basal ganglia-inspired reinforcement learning model
Article.Authors: Bhattacharya, N.; Nair, S. S.; Chakravarthy, V. S.; Muralidharan, V.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) gait is characterized by reduced walking speed, short shuffling steps, increased double stance time, and increased step time variability. The most debilitating symptom in PD is freezing of gait (FOG), a context-dependent locomotion arrest, mostly occurring while encountering turns, obstacles, and narrow pathways. FOG is more pronounced during turning, a complex task that challenges motor planning and execution. Here, we simulate this phenomenon using a computational model inspired by the cortico-basal ganglia circuitry, based on reinforcement learning (RL) principles. In the model, the agent was trained to learn a value profile while navigating a path that involved turning. To simulate PD conditions, we clamped the temporal difference (TD) error, typically associated with dopaminergic signaling. Our model results show that compared to healthy controls (HC), PD non-freezers and PD freezers exhibit a reduction in turning velocity and step length, alongside an attenuated compensatory step-width widening at the sharpest turn, more pronounced in PD freezers, who additionally show increased step time variability. These kinematic impairments worsen during tighter turns. Ultimately, this model implicates FOG as a problem of impaired estimation of value over space and could potentially represent a generalized deficit in gait impairments in PD.

Article.Title: Huntingtin and Celsr3 Orchestrate Spontaneous Long-Distance Spinal Cord Regeneration
Article.Authors: Mathiaparanam, J.; Navarro, M. F.; Granato, M.
Article.Abstract: Spontaneous spinal cord regeneration is an endogenous process operational in diverse vertebrate and select mammalian species. Yet despite resulting in functional regeneration, axonal regrowth dynamics as well as underlying molecular programs are largely unknown. Live-cell imaging following laser axotomy of individual zebrafish spinal cord M-cell axons reveals a time-sensitive multistep process. From a genetic screen we uncover previously unrecognized roles for two evolutionary conserved genes, celsr3 and huntingtin (htt) in spontaneous spinal cord regeneration. Specifically, we find that htt is critical to initiate a transcriptional injury response in regenerating M-cells, enabling their axon to traverse the injury site. Once axons cross the injury site celsr3 functions to increase growth rates, while both celsr3 and htt function to sustain long-range axonal growth. Moreover, we show that htt is dispensable for optic nerve and peripheral motor neuron regeneration, and that reducing soma-to-injury site distance in htt mutant M-cell axons partially restores regeneration, demonstrating a selective role in long-range CNS axon regeneration. Consistent with a transport-based mechanism, genetic knockdown of htt-associated axonal transport proteins recapitulates the htt mutant regeneration phenotype. Combined, our results provide compelling evidence for a time and distance-sensitive multistep molecular framework in which celsr3 dependent growth rate modulation and htt dependent axonal transport promote spontaneous, long-range spinal cord regeneration.

Article.Title: Physiologically relevant metrics for evaluating photoreceptor signal reproduction in visual displays
Article.Authors: Schneider, A. C.; Morimoto, T.; Smithson, H. E.; Spitschan, M.
Article.Abstract: The colour gamut of a display defines the range of colour signals that it can reproduce. For human vision this range is typically visualized in a colour space that reflects the spectral sensitivities of the cone photoreceptors. While the cones dominate canonical visual function (i.e. perception of colour, form, and motion) under photopic light levels, rods and melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) also respond to light. Three-primary display technologies, with their focus on reproducing colour, are not designed to control the rod and melanopsin excitations. As a result, conventional display metrics do not capture the ability of the display to reproduce the full human physiological response to light. In this paper, two physiologically relevant metrics are proposed for quantifying the reproduction and distortion of the photoreceptor signals by visual displays. An equal-luminance photoreceptor excitation diagram is proposed, extending the MacLeod-Boynton chromaticity diagram, providing three-dimensional projections of the five-dimensional photoreceptor signal space to help with visualization. Each metric and visualisation quantifies a specific aspect of the reproducibility of real-world spectra, analogous to the colour rendering index. To demonstrate their application, we use these tools to assess both real and hypothetical displays across tens of thousands of radiance spectra derived from real-world reflectance samples under various illuminants.

Article.Title: LLM-powered automatic scoring tools for memory recall
Article.Authors: Tang, R. S.; Born, S. J.; Delarazan, A. I.; Demarest, P. L.; Karagoz, A. B.; Reagh, Z. M.
Article.Abstract: Free recall of naturalistic stimuli, such as films and stories, reveals what people remember and how they organize it. Scoring such recall requires matching each recalled utterance to the encoded stimulus, and doing this manually often makes large studies impractical. Existing automated methods mostly return similarity or aggregate scores rather than explicit matches between recalled and stimulus content. Here we introduce an open-source, model-agnostic pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to divide the stimulus and the recall into information units and to match units between the two texts. The output is a table of unit-to-unit matches with accuracy labels, from which standard analysis scripts compute recall measures. We validated the pipeline with four LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT 5.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Gemini 2.5 Flash) on three datasets. On typed recall of four short stories, agreement between each model and two trained raters ({phi} = .73-.79) was close to the agreement between the raters themselves ({phi} = .77). A second run reproduced each model's matches ({phi} = .91-.97) more closely than the raters agreed with each other. On spoken recall of 10 films, every model attributed recall to the correct film with high agreement. On uncorrected speech-to-text recall of a television episode, agreement varied more across models. The median cost was under $1 per participant for every model. These results suggest that the pipeline can serve as a reliable, low-cost alternative to manual scoring of free recall.

Article.Title: Neural circuit mechanisms for multi-tasking
Article.Authors: Beiran, M.; Marschall, O.; Zemlianova, K.; Di Bernardo, A.; Ostojic, S.; Litwin-Kumar, A.
Article.Abstract: Neural activity during performance of a cognitive or motor task is often described as lying on a low-dimensional manifold in the space of all possible activity patterns. When multiple tasks are performed, an individual brain region's activity may generate multiple such manifolds. Several models have been introduced to explain this capability, each with different assumptions concerning architecture and inputs. Here, we develop a theory of multi-tasking according to which models and experimental paradigms can be organized. We introduce a distinction between sequential and simultaneous multi-tasking, the performance of one task at a time or multiple in parallel. We show that interference between tasks often prevents multi-tasking and introduce a model of ``task barcodes" that circumvents this problem and parameterizes a neuronal population's task selectivity. Our theory reveals categorical distinctions between neural circuit mechanisms supporting multi-tasking that can be probed using physiological recordings.

Article.Title: Flexible 3D multimodal organoid interface reveals functional subnetworks and coordinated circuit activity in cortical organoids
Article.Authors: Wilson, M. N.; Kharitonova, E. K.; Yeh, J.; Lee, J.; Hemaidan, S.; Essig, S.; Shi, M.; Crain, C. W.; Ramezani, M.; Sun, F.; Zhou, T.; Surucu, I.; Mortazavi, F.; Cubukcu, E.; Thunemann, M.; Zeldich, E.; Kuzum, D.
Article.Abstract: The balance between excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) neurons is fundamental to cortical function, and its disruption underlies a wide range of neurological disorders, including epilepsy, Alzheimers disease and autism spectrum disorder. Cortical organoids offer a promising model to study this balance, as they recapitulate key features of brain development, including the emergence of E/I circuitry. However, no existing technology can simultaneously resolve neuronal identity, spatial organization, and dynamic network activity within intact organoids, limiting precise interrogation of E/I circuit function. Here, we report INFORM, an INtegrated Flexible Organoid Recording Multimodal neural interface that conformally wraps organoids of any size and shape, enabling long-term recordings over 371 days with above 90% of channels detecting spikes. INFORM interface combines four distinct modalities; electrophysiology, two-photon calcium imaging, targeted electrical microstimulation, and chemical intervention to monitor and modulate neural activity across multiple spatial and temporal scales spanning from action potentials from single neurons to synchronized bursts from large-scale populations. Such high-resolution interrogation enables probing of emergence of functional connectivity in fusing assembloids and resolves spatially discrete functional subnetworks that can be selectively recruited and modulated by INFORM. Neurotransmission blockade confirms that stimulus-evoked suppression of neuronal spiking is mediated by GABAergic inputs providing direct functional evidence of the presence of inhibitory signaling in organoids. This work allows single-cell dissection of functional networks in brain organoids, providing a powerful platform for modelling and studying cortical development, neurological diseases, and the E/I imbalances underlying circuit dysfunction.

Article.Title: Self-Exciting Population Event Models Reveal Abnormal Temporal Amplification in MAPT-Mutant Human Brain Assembloids
Article.Authors: Monsoor, T.; McCrimmon, C. M.; Sinha, P.; Zhang, L.; Dareddy, M. R.; Lorasdagi, M. E.; Samarasinghe, R. A.; Roychowdhury, V.
Article.Abstract: Human brain assembloids provide a tractable platform for studying mutation-specific network dysfunction, but most studies do not distinguish whether abnormal activity arises from increased spontaneous initiation or stronger history-dependent amplification. We introduce a low-dimensional discrete-time self-exciting population model for calcium-imaging event sequences that separates baseline initiation (%[mu]), integrated history-dependent gain (%[eta]), and memory decay (%[tau]). Across 175 recordings from 13 MAPT p.R406W or CRISPR-corrected isogenic assembloids, biological-unit inference identified a 4.31-fold increase in %[eta] in mutants (95% CI 3.20- 5.84; exact p=7.8x10-4), without increased baseline activity. Parametric predictive checks exposed residual Poisson overdispersion; fixed-decay and beta-binomial sensitivity analyses nevertheless preserved the mutant history effect. Median %[eta] separated all 13 held-out assembloids, while a multifeature recording-level RBF-SVM achieved AUC 0.816 under nested whole-assembloid holdout. These results identify robust history-dependent temporal amplification as a functional MAPT-mutant network phenotype.

Article.Title: Direction-sensitive neural correlates of voluntary pain regulation: regional response attenuation during down-regulation and exploratory prefrontal-valuation coupling
Article.Authors: Kharghani, M.; Gholami, E.
Article.Abstract: Voluntary cognitive regulation can increase or decrease pain, but direction-sensitive neural correlates may emerge at different analytical levels. We reanalyzed 3,201 thermal-stimulation trials from 33 participants, integrating 0-200 warmth/pain ratings, regional fMRI activity, and trial-wise lagged coupling. Both instructions shifted ratings in the intended direction, with no reliable difference in mean success. Down-regulation was associated with lower bilateral S2/opercular and insular activity and higher left dlPFC/IFJ activity after FDR correction across 32 regions; run-matched comparisons were weaker and none survived the corresponding correction. Contrast-map Neurologic Pain Signature attenuation did not replicate in a rating-adjusted FWL-LSS trial-wise analysis despite strong temperature sensitivity. Up-regulation success covaried with an exploratory, post selection lagged dlPFC/IFJ-valuation composite (r = -0.546, 95% CI [-0.764, -0.270]). The association exceeded matched reverse-direction, zero-lag, and time-reversed controls, lay outside permutation and circular-shift nulls, and persisted after AR(1) prewhitening. A transition-level analysis across 297 up-regulation transitions preserved a negative success-by-source interaction (adjusted three-target mean beta = -0.163, cluster-bootstrap 95% CI [-0.290, -0.054], Freedman-Lane p = 0.010). Six session-wise DCM variants showed no consistent regulation-versus-passive effective-connectivity effect and did not independently validate an up-specific directed mechanism. These analyses identify a down-regulation-associated regional pattern and a candidate prefrontal-valuation coupling association requiring independent confirmation.

Article.Title: Selective vulnerability of intracortical projection neurons drives long-term cortical circuit rewiring after perinatal hypoxia
Article.Authors: Ellouze, S.; Babina, E.; Meyer-Dilhet, G.; Foucault, L.; Amara, A.; Desmerciere, S.; Gagnieu, T.; Mongellaz, S.; Cataldi, A.; Marcy, G.; Ghersi-Egea, J. F.; Courchet, J.; Raineteau, O.
Article.Abstract:
Cortical circuits are built at perinatal times and gradually refined in an activity-dependent manner during a so-called postnatal period of critical plasticity. Although lesions of the central nervous system (CNS) happening during this period typically recover better than those occurring later in life, they are often associated with long-term behavioral deficits. This suggests that neuronal circuits rewiring, in particular within the cortex, may either be incomplete or inappropriate.
To address this possibility, we used chronic perinatal hypoxia, a mouse model of very premature birth. We confirmed that chronic hypoxia induced a decrease in cortical thickness frequently observed in very preterm babies, which rapidly recovered 8 days later. To explore the transcriptional correlates of this recovery we next performed singlenuclei transcriptomic analysis of the cortex at short (P11) and long (P45) timepoints following hypoxia. This revealed persistent transcriptional changes within neurons, including of genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism, axonogenesis and synaptogenesis. Further, histological analysis using anterograde and retrograde tracing as well as mitochondrial labelling support persistent alterations in upper cortical neurons resulting in increased corticocortical connectivity within the cortex of adult hypoxic mice. Finally, behavioral testing revealed altered social behavior in mice exposed to chronic hypoxia, which amplified with age.
Altogether, our results unravel how brain lesions happening early in life, alter normal cortical development and have long term consequences on cortical wiring, contributing to the observed behaviors defects appearing later in life.

Article.Title: Motivational incentives improve working memory performance by enhancing memory-based representations rather than altering response strategies
Article.Authors: Nair, V.; Agnel, O.; Mizrak, E.; Manohar, S. G.
Article.Abstract: Motivational incentives are known to improve working memory (WM) when items differ in value, but whether they enhance performance when all items are equally valued, and if so, by what mechanism, remains unclear. Improvements could reflect enhanced memory-based representations or speed-accuracy trade-offs, whereby incentives promote slower, more cautious responding without improving memory itself. Here, we tested these alternatives across two experiments using an auditory WM task in which incentives varied across trials, but all items on a trial were equally incentivised. In Experiment 1,we allowed participants to resubmit their responses if desired. Reward-related improvements in WM performance were selectively observed when memory load was high, and only at serial positions associated with greater interference. These improvements were also dissociated from systematic response slowing and resubmission behaviour. This indicated that the benefits of incentives were unlikely to be attributable to response caution. Critically, in Experiment 2, motivational benefits persisted under strict response deadlines, where speed cannot be traded for accuracy. Computational modelling showed that reward selectively improved the precision of memory-based responses without reducing guessing. Together, these findings indicate that motivational incentives improve WM by enhancing the quality of memory-based representations, rather than by strategic slowing or altering response strategies.

Article.Title: Associations Between Neural Responses to Social Fairness and Financial Exploitation Vulnerability Vary With Age and Emotional Intelligence
Article.Authors: Stanley, J. M.; Sazhin, D.; Helion, C.; Giovannetti, T.; Fareri, D.; Smith, D. V.
Article.Abstract: Financial exploitation often arises in social contexts in which individuals must evaluate fairness, trust, and interpersonal information during financial decisions. We examined whether neural responses to fairness in social versus nonsocial contexts relate to financial exploitation vulnerability and whether these relationships vary with age, emotional intelligence, and affect. A total of 310 adults spanning ages 21-89 completed an fMRI Ultimatum Game in which they accepted or rejected offers from human and computer partners, along with measures of financial exploitation vulnerability, emotional intelligence, and affect. Participants were strongly sensitive to offer fairness, and individual differences in behavioral sensitivity to partner type were associated with social-relative anterior insula responses to unfairness. Greater baseline negative affect was associated with stronger anterior insula differentiation between social and nonsocial fairness. Financial exploitation vulnerability was associated with prefrontal responses to social-relative fairness in ways that depended on individual characteristics: age moderated its association with dorsomedial prefrontal cortex activation, whereas emotional intelligence moderated its association with dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation. Whole-brain connectivity analyses further showed that age moderated associations between emotional intelligence and executive control network connectivity with posterior cingulate and right temporoparietal regions. These findings suggest that vulnerability to financial exploitation is reflected in how social context is integrated with affective and individual characteristics across adulthood.

Article.Title: Trial-History and Spatial Biases Shape Perceptual Decision-Making in Archerfish
Article.Authors: Hendler, O.; Mondal, k.; Dushnik Shamir, N.; Volotsky, S.; Shamir, M.; Segev, R.
Article.Abstract: Identifying conserved principles of animal decision-making requires comparisons across evolutionarily distant species with divergent neuroanatomy. Yet teleost fish, an evolutionarily distant vertebrate lineage lacking a laminated cortex, are rarely studied using behavioral paradigms directly comparable to those used in mammals and birds. Here, we bridge this gap by exploiting the unique hunting behavior of archerfish to investigate determinants of decision-making. We trained archerfish to report their choices by shooting a jet of water at the selected visual target in a series of two-alternative choice tasks. We found that archerfish decisions are influenced by trial-history and spatial-biases, remarkably similar to those observed in mammalian and avian models. Specifically, subjects exhibited an outcome-history in the form of stay/switch behaviors, alongside a stimulus-history bias, in which they repeatedly selected the same shape across trials. Yet, unlike rodents, archerfish maintained stable behavior during unrewarded probe trials. Thus, our findings reveal that several fundamental determinants of choice previously characterized primarily in mammals are also present in teleost fish, suggesting that important components of vertebrate decision-making are conserved despite substantial divergence in brain organization and ecology. Simultaneously, the distinct response of archerfish to reward omission highlights species-specific differences in how animals adapt to changing environmental contingencies.

Article.Title: Dietary magnesium supplement enhances memory through Hippo signaling
Article.Authors: Wu, Y.; Treiber, C. D.; Waddell, S.
Article.Abstract: Dietary magnesium (Mg2+) supplement enhances memory in mammals and Drosophila, but whether and how Mg2+ changes molecular states of neurons, remains unknown. Here we used single-cell RNA sequencing to map cell-type specific transcriptional responses to memory-enhancing dietary Mg2+. These analyses revealed changes in Hippo-pathway gene expression in memory-relevant {beta} Kenyon Cells (KCs) of the mushroom bodies. Targeted knock-down of Merlin, hippo (hpo) and warts demonstrated requirement in {beta} KCs for Mg2+-enhanced, but not baseline memory. Further study of Hippo signaling identified Yorkie (yki) transcriptional coactivator and DNA-binding partner Scalloped (sd) to be required for baseline and Mg2+-enhanced memory. Moreover, releasing Yki::Sd of inhibition from Tondu-domain containing growth inhibitor (Tgi) specifically in {beta} KCs enhanced memory, independent of diet. Analyses of Yki::Sd target genes identified several required in {beta} KCs for baseline memory, including crb and Glut1 which are also Mg2+-induced in a Hippo-dependent manner in {beta} KCs. These genes suggest that aiding the metabolic demands of long-term memory and facilitating structural neuronal plasticity are key mediators of Mg2+-induced memory enhancement. We propose pharmacological enhancement of Sd-dependent transcription, and activity of particular Sd-target genes may have therapeutic potential for memory disorders.

Article.Title: Emergent critical oscillations in motor cortex of Parkinson's patients
Article.Authors: Ly, C.; Sooter, J. S.; Barreiro, A.; Fontenele, A. J.; Shew, W.
Article.Abstract: The dynamical state of cortical neural activity constrains the complexity of functions it can perform. A marginally stable dynamical state - called criticality - is thought to be beneficial for brain functions that require multiple time scales, broad dynamic range, and large information storage and transmission. A growing body of evidence suggests that criticality is a feature of healthy brain dynamics, but breaks down in certain brain disorders. Here we ask whether Parkinson's disease incurs deviation from criticality compared to healthy controls. We analyze human resting state EEG activity in primary motor cortex. Parkinson's patients exhibit prominent oscillatory brain activity in multiple frequency bands (low delta and high theta) that is not present in controls. Surprisingly, we find that these emergent oscillations are close to criticality, i.e., amplitude fluctuations with approximate temporal scale invariance. We compare traditional signatures of criticality and more principled measurements of proximity to criticality using our new approach based on information theory using temporal renormalization group. Our new approach and traditional methods agree, demonstrating that critical dynamics are not always associated with healthy states; Parkinson's disease is associated with the emergence of near-critical oscillations in motor cortex.

Article.Title: Reciprocal control of the stomach and intestine by viscerosensory neurons in caudal brainstem
Article.Authors: Dundar, N.; Alkislar, I.; Jarvie, B. C.; Namkung, H.; Xie, K.; Kaur, M.; Li, Q.; Ravi, A. S.; Lopez, A.; Spina, A.; Qui, L.; Ly, T.; Oh, J.; Yackle, K.; Knight, Z. A.
Article.Abstract: Digestion requires precisely timed transit of food through the gastrointestinal tract. Here we show that emptying of food from the stomach occurs in discrete pulses, separated by pauses that allow the proximal duodenum to clear before the next bolus arrives. By combining X-ray fluoroscopy of the gut with calcium imaging of the brainstem, we identify a population of neurons defined by expression of neuropeptide FF (NPFF) that tracks these duodenal dynamics. Stimulation of NPFF neurons induces a coordinated response that inhibits gastric emptying and accelerates intestinal transit, thereby clearing the proximal intestine for the next bolus of food. These neurons also bidirectionally control food intake through cholinergic signaling in the gut. These findings reveal a mechanism by which brainstem transforms the sensory detection of nutrients in the duodenum into the opposing control of the stomach and intestine. They also establish an experimental approach for dissecting gut-brain signaling in behaving animals.

Article.Title: Rate of functional network maturity and the role of environmental factors
Article.Authors: Hughes-Small, B.; Saljoughi, S.; Stevenson, R. A.; Soddu, A.; Stojanoski, B.
Article.Abstract: The developmental period from childhood to adolescence is marked by significant changes to brain function that support higher-level cognition. Environmental factors such as socioeconomic status and adversity can have an outsized but distinct influences on neurocognitive development. Here, we examined the differential influences of SES (i.e., parental education and neighbourhood safety) and adversity on the maturation rate of functional networks in children and adolescents. Using resting-state fMRI data, independent component analysis with dual regression was computed to identify six networks (Default Mode Network (DMN), Left Executive Control Network (ECN), Right ECN, Hippocampal (HPC), Salience, and Sensorimotor networks) of interest in children and adolescents aged 7 to 15 (N=216, acquired from the Healthy Brain Network). A neural maturity index was generated based on the degree of similarity between the spatial configuration of each networks in every youth brain to that of a sex-matched adult template. Regression analyses were used to determine the association between neural maturity, environmental factors, and social-cognitive abilities. We found one sensory (sensorimotor) and two association (default mode and executive control) networks matured faster than other networks. Only the rate of maturity of the DMN and HPC were associated with environmental factors. Maturity of the DMN was associated with less adversity and better social cognitive ability, whereas maturity of the HPC network was associated with younger participants with higher IQs. Moreover, these effects were stronger in females than males. Our results highlight the importance of examining the unique contributions of distinct dimensions of childhood environments on neurocognitive development.

Article.Title: Social feedback structures stay/switch decision-making in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Aragon, M. J.; Murthy, M.
Article.Abstract: Within natural environments, different sensory stimuli can drive mutually-exclusive behaviors such as fighting, feeding, or courting. When experiencing competing cues, how do animals decide to continue executing the current behavior or to switch to a new behavior? To address this question, we developed a closed-loop behavioral paradigm that presents actively courting male Drosophila with a fictive heat stimulus, forcing the male to choose between two competing behaviors: continue courting (stay) or escape the heat (switch). By modeling the sensorimotor transformations underlying this decision process, we discovered that male flies continually evaluate social cues, including female speed and her distance, in order to make a stay/switch decision. We investigated the neural correlates of stay/switch decision-making via brain-wide calcium imaging in head-fixed male flies presented with both fictive female visual cues and heat stimuli. We built models that predicted stay/switch decisions from neural data, which revealed that activity in a small number of brain regions, including the anterior optic tubercle, predicted decision outcomes up to 4 seconds prior to stimulus onset, whereas after stimulus onset, distributed activity across the brain was correlated with the behavioral decision. Together, these results demonstrate that Drosophila continually evaluate social feedback to inform decisions about how to respond to environmental cues, and that brain activity changes prior to presentation of the environmental cue can inform upcoming decisions. Overall, this study provides new insight into the processes underlying naturalistic decision-making in Drosophila.

Article.Title: Path Integration Promotes Flexible Navigational Decision Making
Article.Authors: Blair, H. T.; Grgurich, R.; Wang, S.; Wang, Y.; Pimenta, J.; Delafraz, K.
Article.Abstract: Flexible decision making depends on internal representations that capture the latent structure of a task, allowing prior knowledge to be applied in novel circumstances. Spatial navigation provides a useful model for studying flexible choice behavior, because spatial location is itself a latent variable that must be inferred rather than directly perceived. Here, we trained rats on a navigation task that required them to reach the same goal via two distinct paths from different starting locations, and then return to one of the two starting locations before beginning the next trial. Some rats were trained to rely on distal visual landmarks, allowing task states to be identified from current sensory information, whereas others were trained to rely on path integration, requiring task states to be inferred from self-motion information accumulated over the preceding trajectory. Rats trained to rely on path integration acquired the task similarly to rats trained to rely on distal visual landmarks. However, reliance on path integration enhanced rats' ability to generalize their learning to novel situations, including finding the goal from an untrained starting location and adapting to a relocated goal that reversed learned choice sequences. These findings suggest that reliance on path integration promotes the acquisition and use of mental representations that capture the latent spatial structure of navigational tasks, thereby favoring flexible navigational decisions over rigid retrieval of reinforced responses. More broadly, our findings demonstrate how information available during training can shape representations learned from experience and thereby constrain the flexibility of decision making during inference.

Article.Title: Dynamically rich states in balanced networks induced by single-neuron dynamics
Article.Authors: Drangmeister, M.; Engelken, R.; Schleimer, J.-H.; Schreiber, S.
Article.Abstract: Network states with rich dynamics and highly variable firing rates of individual neurons are prominent in experimental observations and thought to benefit complex information processing and learning. Such states have been proposed to arise from properties of network coupling, like a strong connectivity or slow synaptic dynamics. Here, we identify an alternative mechanism based on weak synaptic coupling and intrinsic cellular dynamics. We show that a switch in the cellular excitability class of action-potential generation (via a switch in the underlying mathematical bifurcation) results in super-Poissonian spiking variability in random balanced networks, where the recurrent network reinforces rather than averages out the single-cell effect. Information encoding is shifted to higher frequency bands and collective chaos in the network is enhanced when intrinsic cellular dynamics follow a saddle homoclinic orbit (HOM) bifurcation. Entropy production and attractor dimension peak close to the saddle-node-loop point that separates the two excitability classes, pointing to the qualitative nature of the transition as the origin of the effect. Because such switches are induced by common physiological variables, like temperature or extracellular potassium, and leave synaptic weights untouched, they offer a route to setting a network's dynamical regime independently of plasticity. The robust effect links the biophysics of individual neurons to collective dynamics of large random networks, highlighting the relevance of single-cell dynamics for computation in physiological and artificial networks.

Article.Title: Seeing at Will: Shared Neural Representations of Motion Perception and Intention
Article.Authors: Si, W.; Choe, E.; Heller, N. H.; Kohler, P. J.; Cavanagh, P.; Stoermer, V. S.; Tse, P.
Article.Abstract: Intention can bias perception in cases where two or more interpretations of a stimulus are possible. The neural mechanisms whereby intention influences perception are poorly understood. Here we investigated whether the intention to perceive horizontal or vertical motion in a bistable apparent motion stimulus pre-activates motion axes representations in sensory cortex before the position shift occurs and before motion in consciously perceived. Twelve participants underwent fMRI scanning under three conditions: (1) passively viewing quartet stimuli moving continuously along veridical trajectories; (2) passively viewing bistable apparent motion quartet stimuli induced by two pairs of squares alternately flashing at diagonally opposite corners of an invisible rectangle; or (3) while actively intending to perceive a single-shot apparent-motion stimulus as moving either vertically or horizontally. Multivariate decoding analyses revealed that activity patterns during the intention period of (3) generalized to patterns evoked by both (1) physical and (2) ambiguous motion perception. Cross-decoding was strongest within dorsal/lateral visual regions, including hMT+, V3AB, and the intraparietal sulcus, but was largely absent from ventral visual cortex. Widespread overlap was also observed between intention-related and perceptual motion representations throughout the dorsal/lateral visual cortex. Our findings suggest that intention may bias prospective sensory representations prior to the stimulus-driven processing that results in perceptual experience and that these representations closely resemble those associated with illusory motion perception. The fact that intention-related representations were mostly found within dorsal/lateral visual regions is consistent with top-down influences from attentional control systems.

Article.Title: Do monkeys dream about food while sleeping?
Article.Authors: Joby, J.; Simon, S.; Cherian, T.; Jacob, G.; Das, J.; Munda, S.; Saha, S.; Bhadra, D.; Arun, S.
Article.Abstract: Can we tell what animals are dreaming about from their brain activity? This fascinating question has been explored extensively using the rodent hippocampus, where place cells are sequentially reactivated during sleep, consistent with replay of paths explored while awake. However, dreams involve vivid visual experiences, and whether analogous replays occur in the visual cortex has not been explored, that too in primates. To address this gap, we performed wireless neural recordings from the high-level visual (IT) and motor regions (PMv, PFC) in two monkeys while they viewed food images on a screen while awake, and afterwards while they slept in their natural setting. Decoders trained on sleep/wake neural activity in each region were able to accurately predict the ongoing sleep/wake state, as well as upcoming transitions between states. Interestingly, decoders trained to categorize neural responses to food (but not faces/objects) showed increased probability during REM-like sleep compared to NREM or awake states. Thus, behaviorally relevant visual stimuli seen while awake are reactivated during REM-like sleep. In other words, these monkeys saw food, faces and objects while awake, and dreamt selectively about food while sleeping.

Article.Title: Reactive and predictive processes during unpredictable driving collisions in virtual reality: an exploratory immersive study with multimodal neurophysiological monitoring
Article.Authors: Cannard, C.; Yesilbas, D.
Article.Abstract: Anticipatory neurophysiological activity before unpredictable emotional events has been reported for decades, but the effects are small, difficult to replicate, and obtained almost exclusively in stripped-down laboratory paradigms. Whether they reflect genuine predictive processes or methodological artifacts remains debated; one rarely tested possibility is that such settings mute it. We examined anticipation in an immersive virtual reality (VR) driving simulation whose collision outcomes were assigned by a quantum random number generator, while EEG, photoplethysmography (PPG), EMG, EOG and inertial (IMU) signals were recorded from a single wireless dry-electrode headset built into the VR display. Sixteen participants passively observed 120 driving sequences ending in a collision or no collision. Length-matched pre- and post-stimulus windows were analysed identically with mass-univariate hierarchical general linear models under permutation cluster correction, plus machine-learning classification across held-out participants. Two post-stimulus clusters differentiated the conditions, the largest peaking at 451.6 ms (d = -1.35), with broadband power modulation robust to baseline modelling, decoded from held-out participants with up to 93.8% accuracy. No time-domain effect or decodable information preceded stimulus onset, but a broadband spectral difference did, surviving preregistered controls for expectation bias (run length), time-on-task build-up and ocular or facial-muscle artifact: directionally consistent in 13 of 15 participants, with pre- and post-stimulus power coupled in all 16. Heart rate differentiated the conditions neither alone nor when added to the classifier. The study was preregistered; the BIDS-format data, analysis code and an open-source EEGLAB plugin are publicly available.

Article.Title: Information regimes in population-graph neuroimaging: cohort context and implementation-dependent evaluation sensitivity
Article.Authors: Chen, Z.; Yu, B.; Wan, K.; Zhang, Q.; Zhang, F.; Zhong, N.; Kuai, H.
Article.Abstract: Population-graph models aggregate a query subject with an unlabeled cohort, so their reported performance can depend on the evaluation regime rather than on predictive information alone. Evaluation context has two separable axes: the visibility of the cohort during training, and the context available at inference. We study the training-time axis under a protocol fixed before analysis, on an ABIDE-I cohort of 871 subjects (20 acquisition sites). Two population-graph implementations are compared: a learned/adaptive graph (EV-GCN) and a static weighted graph (Parisot-GCN). Within each implementation the cohort, connectivity features, outer splits and training and selection rules are held fixed, and only the information available to the graph varies. The primary estimand is the implementation-by-training-context interaction: the difference between the P0-to-P1 AUC changes of the two implementations ({Delta}{Delta}AUC). Across three preselected outer splits (666, 1024, 2024) the direction is consistent and positive, with observed interaction range 0.06285-0.13090; uncertainty is assessed separately within each split by paired subject and site-cluster bootstrap resampling and is reported per split. Splits are replication units: they are not pooled and no cross-split average is reported, so the result is not a claim of invariance to arbitrary splits. These findings tie reported population-graph performance to the evaluation information regime and motivate explicit reporting of cohort visibility. The contribution is methodological: a two-axis taxonomy of information regimes, preselected cross-split evidence that the sensitivity of reported performance to cohort context depends on the implementation, and a reusable reporting checklist.

Article.Title: Retinal cell mosaics in the valproate-induced rat model of autism spectrum disorder
Article.Authors: Telkes, I.; Fusz, K.; Janosi, T. Z.; Kobor, P.; ElZafarany, A.; Sari, Z.; Laszlo, K.; Buzas, P.
Article.Abstract: Valproic acid (VPA) is a widely used antiepileptic drug that also increases the risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in the offspring of exposed mothers. Prenatal exposure to VPA is a widely used rodent model of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Anatomical, functional and molecular alterations in the retinas of various ASD model animals have been described, but the impact on the neural composition of the retina remains unclear. We examined whether the density and spatial regularity of selected retinal neuron populations are altered in the VPA induced model of ASD. Whole-mount retinas of 2-month-old VPA-treated and control animals were immunolabeled for S-cones, horizontal cells, AII amacrine cells, and parvalbumin-positive wide-field amacrine cells (PV-wfACs), and the positions of labelled cells mapped in various regions of interest across the retina. Multivariate analysis of the densities of the four cell types was used to identify latent factors accounting for their covariance structure. The first principal component was identified as a measure of retinal centrality and used to adjust for retinal location when testing for treatment effects. Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed a 9% decrease in AII amacrine cell density and a 12% increase in PV-wfACs density in VPA-model animals. Regularity indices calculated from nearest neighbor distances or Voronoi-domain areas of cell mosaics were largely unchanged. These findings suggest that prenatal VPA exposure selectively alters the cellular composition of inhibitory inner retinal circuitry in the rat ASD model, while leaving the self-organizing mechanisms responsible for retinal spatial order largely intact.

Article.Title: Ringer Loss in <Drosophila/> Uncovers Mitochondrial Complex I Deficits Relevant to Human Parkinson's Disease
Article.Authors: Tillmon, H. G.; Boyen, S. K.; Velazquez, R.; Urbina-Berlanga, M. E.; Sciortino, M.; Banerjee, S.
Article.Abstract: Tubulin polymerization promoting proteins (TPPPs) are known for their cytoskeletal regulation across species; however, emerging evidence suggests broader cellular functions, including potential roles in mitochondrial biology. Here, we identify the Drosophila homolog of human TPPP, Ringer, as a previously unrecognized regulator of mitochondrial bioenergetics and electron transport chain Complex I (CI) function. Ringer is enriched in the mitochondrial matrix, and its loss results in reduced levels of multiple CI subunits and assembly factors and a significant decrease in CI enzymatic activity. Notably, in addition to TPPP dysfunction, similar deficits are observed in postmortem human Parkinson's disease (PD) brain tissues, underscoring the translational relevance of our Drosophila model. Pharmacological administration of resveratrol, a reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenger, reduces mitochondrial superoxide levels and improves CI enzymatic activity and ATP production in ringer mutants, demonstrating that targeted antioxidant therapeutics can improve bioenergetic functions in ringer mutants. Together, these findings establish Ringer as a key regulator of mitochondrial bioenergetics and reveal Ringer-induced CI dysfunction as a phenotype relevant to mitochondrial abnormalities observed in PD, and provide a robust and translationally meaningful framework for investigating mitochondrial dysfunction in PD.

Article.Title: An AI-Enabled Translational Drug Discovery Framework for NALCN Channelopathy: From High-Throughput Screening to Therapeutic Candidate
Article.Authors: Thongsepee, N.; Tanner, J. A.; Polusani, S.; Typou, A.; Clanton, N. A.; Holmes, B. B.; Lory, P.; Dwyer, D. S.; Zhou, D.; Monteil, A.; Yuan, Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: More than 90% of rare diseases lack an approved therapy, partly reflecting economic barriers in developing treatments for small patient populations. A common bottleneck is costly and resource-intensive hit-to-lead prioritization. Congenital contractures of the limbs and face, hypotonia, and developmental delay (CLIFAHDD) is an ultra-rare neurodevelopmental disease often caused by de novo gain-of-function variants in the sodium leak channel NALCN, with no approved treatments. Methods: We developed a cost and resource-efficient, AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic high-throughput screening (HTS), structural biology foundation models for hit-to-lead prioritization, and orthogonal experimental validation. We applied this framework for drug repurposing to identify NALCN inhibitors as therapeutic candidates for CLIFAHDD. We screened ~1,200 approved drugs using a fluorescence-based membrane potential assay in doxycycline-inducible HEK293 cells stably expressing the NALCN channelosome. Boltz-2 modeling predicted binding affinity and mode to prioritize hits. Lead repurposing candidates were selected by a multidisciplinary expert review panel. Lead candidates were evaluated using patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells expressing wild-type or CLIFAHDD-associated NALCN variants, primary mouse hippocampal neurons, and a C. elegans NALCN gain-of-function model. Results: HTS identified 11 candidate NALCN inhibitors. Boltz-2 prioritized candidates based on predicted binding affinity and predicted binding within the NALCN pore, consistent with a direct pore-blocking mechanism. Aprepitant emerged as the lead candidate after multidisciplinary evaluation based on its predicted mechanism, pharmacologic properties, blood-brain barrier penetration, established safety profile, and regulatory approval in children and adults. Patch-clamp electrophysiology confirmed partial inhibition of NALCN-mediated sodium leak currents in HEK293 cells (IC50;=2.22 M), with comparable potency against Cav3.1 (IC50=1.63 M). In primary mouse hippocampal neurons, aprepitant reduced sodium leak currents, hyperpolarized resting membrane potential, and decreased spontaneous firing. Aprepitant rescued hyperlocomotor and dystonic phenotypes in a C. elegans gain-of-function NALCN model. There was notable concordance between AI-predicted hits, phenotypic screening hits, and experimental validation. Conclusion: These findings identify aprepitant as a lead therapeutic candidate for CLIFAHDD, and establish an AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic screening, structural modeling, and experimental validation for NALCN channelopathies. This scalable and resource-conscious strategy may accelerate hit-to-lead prioritization and drug discovery for rare and ultra-rare diseases lacking effective therapies.

Article.Title: Mechanistic simulation identifies predictive dose-dependent biomarkers of propofol anesthesia
Article.Authors: Pathak, A.; Brincat, S. L.; Xiong, Y.; Organtzidis, H.; Protter, M.; Du, V.; Strey, H. H.; Mujica-Parodi, L. R.; Miller, E. K.; Granger, R.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how receptor-level modulation reorganizes large-scale brain circuits remains a central challenge in neuropharmacology. Here we introduce a multiscale mechanistic model with explicit core-matrix thalamocortical architecture to examine how propofol reorganizes brainwide activity from individual receptors to systems-level circuits. Crucially, the model did not involve machine learning or statistical fitting to pre-existing anesthesia data. We use the model to simulate the multi-scale effects of propofol, which range from modulation of individual synaptic conductances to widespread alterations of neural spiking, field potentials, and coherence. Without requiring any training on task-specific data, our simulation of sensory processing in a standard auditory oddball paradigm matches independent data from anesthetized and awake behaving macaques. The same simulation, unmodified, also reproduces changes to functional connectivity in anesthetized humans, exhibiting selective attenuation of matrix thalamocortical loops relative to core loops. Most importantly, the simulation identified a previously unknown biomarker of propofol concentration: elevated residual inter-stimulus cortical activity. This dose-dependent biomarker was subsequently confirmed in empirical macaque data, where it had previously gone unnoticed. This simulation-first discovery, arising from mechanistic circuit dynamics rather than statistical comparison of clinical populations, serves as an illustrative example of a broader generative framework that can translate receptor-level modulation into circuit-scale biomarkers with potential applications across predictive neuropharmacology.

Article.Title: Robust brain inspired prediction of speech recognition accuracy across many words, voices, and natural background sounds
Article.Authors: Clonan, A. C.; Stevenson, I. H.; Escabi, M. A.
Article.Abstract:
Although humans generally excel at recognizing speech in noisy natural environments, performance varies widely due to differences in the background acoustics and individual talker attributes such as voice quality, intonation, and pitch. The underlying neural and acoustic factors of this perceptual variability remain elusive, making it an unresolved challenge to predict when speech recognition will succeed or fail. Here, we characterize human speech recognition across a wide range of natural conditions using speech spoken by 326 diverse male and female talkers of multiple ages embedded in 33 unique background noises. Across this vast soundscape, speech recognition is strongly driven by the spectrum and modulation statistics of the noise. Yet, articulatory speech features - including fundamental and formant frequencies - exert categorically distinct modulatory effects on recognition accuracy across the talkers age and gender, and specific words. This perceptual variability is captured by a low-dimensional statistical representation of sounds based on computations that emulate intermediate stages of sound processing and feature extraction in auditory midbrain. A model utilizing these sound summary statistics accurately predicts individual listeners single-trial recognition behavior, accounting for performance variance across individual voices, words, and backgrounds. Thus, speech-in-noise perception across diverse natural conditions relies largely on a simple set of spectrotemporal summary statistics known to be represented by central neural populations.
Significance StatementAlthough humans can easily maintain conversations amidst environmental noise and voice variations, this capacity is severely degraded by hearing impairment and challenges modern speech recognition technologies. This study evaluates human speech recognition across a broad spectrum of environmental noises and diverse speaker demographics. We show that a brain-inspired auditory representation of sounds extracts critical statistical sound features driving human behavior, precisely predicting variations in perceptual accuracy across distinct voices, words, and environmental backgrounds.

Article.Title: Projection-defined ventral tegmental area neurons exhibit distinct molecular adaptations during acute fentanyl withdrawal
Article.Authors: Montemarano, A.; Sohail, H.; Hnilo, M. E.; Fox, L. D.; Briones, A.; Ostman, A. E.; Fox, M. E.
Article.Abstract: Opioid use disorder (OUD) remains a major public health concern, with potent synthetic opioids driving overdose deaths. Understanding how synthetic opioids like fentanyl alter brain circuits to promote persistent use is critical for advancing OUD treatment. The ventral tegmental area (VTA), which projects to several other brain regions including prefrontal cortex (PFC), nucleus accumbens (NAc) and amygdala (Amy), contributes to both the euphoric and dysphoric phases of OUD. Projection target influences the baseline properties and opioid-induced neuroadaptations of VTA neurons, yet less is known about the molecular adaptations that occur across distinct VTA projections during spontaneous opioid withdrawal. Here, we investigated transcriptional responses to acute spontaneous fentanyl withdrawal in projection-defined VTA neurons. Following chronic fentanyl exposure and 24h of spontaneous withdrawal in male and female mice, we sequenced ribosome-associated RNA from VTA neurons projecting to PFC, NAc, or Amy. We found that fentanyl withdrawal produced divergent transcriptional adaptations in VTA neurons projecting to PFC compared with VTA-NAc and VTA-Amy neurons, whereas adaptations in VTA-NAc and VTA-Amy neurons were more concordant. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified fentanyl-responsive modules across VTA projections, with gene ontology analysis linking these modules to distinct biological processes. We further used regulatory enrichment analysis to identify candidate transcriptional regulators associated with fentanyl-responsive co-expression modules. Together, our data demonstrate that VTA neurons undergo distinct molecular adaptations during fentanyl withdrawal based on their projection target, providing new insight into molecular mechanisms relevant to OUD.

Article.Title: Neuron types and distribution of a Drosophila driver line collection
Article.Authors: Mais, L.; Managan, C.; Yarbrough, B.; Hopkins, G. P.; Salinas, J. R.; Lauchie, S. A.; Hirsch, P.; Karg, C.; Saalfeld, S.; Korff, W.; Ihrke, G.; Kainmueller, D.; Meissner, G. W.
Article.Abstract: Cell type designations label uniquely-identifiable groups of related cells that typically function in similar ways. Cell types divide the Drosophila melanogaster central nervous system into functional units, but remain challenging to target and identify. Previously we generated a driver line and image resource for targeting many neuron types (Meissner et al., 2025). Here we improve on identifying the targeted neurons by automated searching against electron microscopy datasets and manual scoring of search results to add 6,368 annotations across 1,772 driver lines in the collection. These annotations provide a potential training resource for future search algorithms. We then estimate the number of cell types and thus the fraction of the central nervous system labeled by the collection as a whole.

Article.Title: Neuronal sex identity shapes social buffering of defensive freezing behaviour in fruit flies
Article.Authors: Heinemans, M.; Goncalves, R. M.; Moita, M. A.; Ferreira, C. H.
Article.Abstract: Sex differences are pervasive across the animal kingdom1,2, shaped by reproductive strategies, ecological roles, and physiological demands. Neurobiological studies have largely focused on sex differences in reproduction and aggression3,4, leaving understudied how sex shapes other survival-relevant behaviours such as responses to predatory threats. Previous work in vertebrates uncovered sex differences in individual defence responses deployed by rats5 and in social modulation of freezing responses in zebrafish6. The origin of these differences and their potential underlying neuronal circuitry remain however unknown. Here we characterise defensive responses to a visual threat of female and male fruit flies tested alone and in groups. Individually, defensive responses are comparable across sex, with similar freezing levels and moderately increased escape responses in males. In groups, however, we uncovered strong sex differences in freezing as males show consistently shorter freezing bouts, reflecting a stronger social buffering effect than in females. Using a generalised linear mixed model, we demonstrate that the shorter freezes of male flies, when tested in groups, are not explained by well-known locomotor differences between sexes7,8. Although males move more and faster, generating stronger social motion cues that mediate the "safety in numbers" effect in female flies9,10, their response to the surrounding motion is not increased. We further identify the nervous system as the source of this sex-dimorphic behaviour by feminising males through pan-neuronal ectopic expression of transformer, a key regulator of the cell-autonomous sex-differentiation pathway. Finally, we ruled out the visual projection neurons, lobula columnar neurons 11 (LC11), detectors of social motion10, as the source of the neuronal-sex differences observed. This study identifies a neuronal origin of sex differences in socially modulated behaviour that extends beyond sex-specific behavioural modules or locomotor function, important to understand differential impact on survival upon threat across sexes.

Article.Title: Lateral recurrence dynamically refines visual representations for task performance
Article.Authors: Farzmahdi, A.; Adeli, H.; Boran, W.; King, C.; Kriegeskorte, N.
Article.Abstract: Recurrent connections are pervasive in visual cortex, and visual representations evolve as recurrent processing unfolds. Yet the mechanism underlying this temporal transformation remains poorly understood. To address this question, we trained recurrent convolutional networks on face and object recognition and tested them on a parametric stimulus set in which category, identity, and pose were systematically varied. This design isolates how lateral recurrence reshapes neural-population representational geometry and single-unit tuning across recurrent timesteps. Within the trained domain, recurrence increased the separability between identities in deeper layers, while leaving the non-trained domain representations largely unchanged. Gating lateral weights abolished the across-timestep gain in trained-domain identity decoding, demonstrating that lateral recurrence drives this refinement. At the single-unit level, recurrence strengthened the correlation between each unit's category preference and its within-domain identity sensitivity, providing a unit-level mechanism for the population-level changes. These results identify lateral recurrence as a dynamic mechanism for refining learned representational structure within a fixed neural population, yielding testable predictions for time-resolved recordings in domain-selective cortex.

Article.Title: Microstructural heterogeneity of white-matter aging and its age-dependent coupling to cognition
Article.Authors: Chin, R.; Hu, X.; Ranieri, J.; Kim, J.-H.; Oh, H.
Article.Abstract: Brain white matter (WM) microstructure undergoes extensive changes with age, yet the regional and cellular heterogeneity of age-related WM alterations and their impact on cognition remain unclear. Leveraging Neurite Orientation Dispersion and Density Imaging (NODDI), an advanced microstructural modelling to capture specific WM cellular properties, we investigated age-dependent relationships between advanced microstructural markers and cognitive performance, indexed by six cognitive domains derived from principal component analysis. Using a suite of standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and NODDI techniques in eighty-six cognitively normal adults (Young: n=33, Older: n=53), we show that age group differences are widespread across whole brain white matter, with converging region-based and voxel-level evidence implicating commissural, association, and limbic pathways. Older adults exhibited significant and widespread reductions in global fractional anisotropy (FA) and neurite density index (NDI), concomitant with increases in mean diffusivity (MD), orientation density index (ODI), and free water fraction (FWF). Critically, age moderated WM-cognition associations in a domain- and tract-specific manner: younger adults exhibited stronger coupling between commissural and association tract microstructure and language and visual memory, whereas older adults showed greater dependence on projection and limbic tracts for executive and language function. The observed age-dependent coupling between specific microstructural metrics and cognition underscores the value of advanced diffusion models for capturing heterogeneity in brain aging, reveals age-specific biomarkers of cognitive health. These patterns align with phylogenetic and ontogenetic patterns of white matter vulnerability in callosal, long-range association, and limbic pathways, and suggest cellular specificity in white matter changes associated with cognitive decline.

Article.Title: Pharmacokinetic properties of Ogerin and its regulation of post-ischemia signaling in mice
Article.Authors: Zhou, Y.; Joshi, S.; Zha, X.-m.
Article.Abstract: Ogerin, a positive regulator of GPR68, reduces infarct volume and attenuates blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage post transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). These data support the potential use of Ogerin for ischemic protection. For therapeutic interventions, tissue distribution, kinetics, and brain penetration are important characteristics for a compound. For these reasons, we performed liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis of Ogerin in mice. At 3 hours following intraperitoneal (IP) injection, liver exhibited highest level of Ogerin among all major organs assessed. We further analyzed time-dependent changes in Ogerin concentration in serum following intravenous delivery. Brain Ogerin level was ~140 ng/g at 2 hour and ~0.06ng/g at 24 hours. The brain-to-serum ratio of Ogerin was ~0.6 at 5 hr. To determine the effect of Ogerin on signaling, we collected samples 24 hours after tMCAO with or without Ogerin delivered and performed Western blotting. Consistent with the diminished level of Ogerin in brain at 24 hour, tMCAO increased similar changes in phosphorylation of PKA substrates and PKC substrates in vehicle- and Ogerin-treated groups. The pharmacokinetic data suggests that Ogerin is effective mainly during acute hours after injection. This finding generates important insights on the design of effective protocol for Ogerin delivery to potentiate GPR68 function in vivo.

Article.Title: Learning Interpretable Switching Dynamics in Shared Neural-Behavioral Latent Space
Article.Authors: Zhang, Y.; Caro, J. O.; Oren, R.; Higley, M. J.; Cardin, J.; Churchland, A.; Saxena, S.
Article.Abstract: Modern recording technologies enable simultaneous measurement of high-dimensional neural activity and rich behavioral variables, creating both an opportunity and a modeling challenge: identifying the shared latent structure that mediates the brain-behavior relationship and the underlying dynamics through which it evolves across behavioral states. Existing approaches focus on different parts of this challenge: shared representation learning methods identify neural-behavioral subspaces but typically do not model dynamical structure, while dynamical models capture temporal variation and discrete state transitions in neural activity, but do not explicitly disentangle shared neural-behavioral structure from modality-specific variability. We introduce Switching Shared Latent Dynamics (SSLD), a unified framework that learns a latent representation shared between neural activity and behavior and endows this shared space with nonlinear switching recurrent dynamics to reflect the hypothesis that behaviorally relevant neural representations exhibit structured dynamical changes across behavioral states. Complementary private latent variables capture modality-specific variability, providing a window into neural activity that does not directly interact with behavior. We evaluate SSLD on a simulated dataset and four diverse experimental datasets spanning species, brain regions, and recording modalities: monkey motor and premotor cortex during reaching, somatosensory cortex during a bump task, widefield calcium imaging across mouse dorsal cortex during (a) self-initiated decision-making and (b) spontaneous movements. Across all four datasets, SSLD accurately reconstructs neural and behavioral signals, recovers discrete states in the dynamics that align with experimentally defined behavioral epochs, and isolates behaviorally-relevant neural information in the shared latent while preserving private neural variability. Ablations confirm that shared representation learning, behavioral supervision, and switching dynamics each contribute to performance. SSLD offers an interpretable approach to modeling shared neural-behavioral dynamics that complements ongoing efforts toward foundation models for neuroscience.

Article.Title: A network model of path control
Article.Authors: Osman, M. A. M.; Zhang, W.; Pehlevan, C.; Wilson, R. I.
Article.Abstract: We present a network model that enables a navigating agent to shape the spatial and temporal structure of its paths through its environment. The model is inspired by the insect fan-shaped body. In it, a recurrent neural network receives an input that encodes an agent's velocity vector. Meanwhile, network activity determines the setpoint of a control loop that influences this velocity vector through motor outputs. The network thus guides future movement using memory of past movement. We illustrate how the network's dynamics determine the trajectory features it extracts to produce the setpoint. We then relate the joint dynamics of network activity and the agent's velocity vector to the structure of the resulting paths. This network can produce paths suitable for different forms of exploration. It can also stabilize movements initiated by lower-level systems. Our analyses illustrate how recurrent neural dynamics and memory can shape behavior when embedded in closed loops.

Article.Title: Moving object generates topographic responses in the majority of entorhinal neurons
Article.Authors: Purandare, C. S.; Durand, S.; Hardcastle, B.; Gillis, R.; Carlson, M.; Belski, H.; Peene, C.; Bawany, A.; Jha, S.; Amaya, A.; Ha, V.; Han, W.; Ouellette, B.; Johnson, T.; Naidoo, R.; Nguyen, K.; Suarez, L.; Wilkes, J.; Young, A.; Caldejon, S.; Swapp, J.; Williford, A.; Groblewski, P.; Lecoq, J.; Mehta, M. R.
Article.Abstract: Vision is crucial in generating a complex array of responses in rodents during spatial exploration and in humans during memory tasks. These tasks involve other variables too, e.g. multisensory cues in rodents and complex memories in humans. Further, there are major differences between the medial and lateral entorhinal cortical (MEC and LEC) functional cell types. To understand the contribution of purely visual information to entorhinal responses, we presented a simple, moving vertical bar of light to head-fixed mice, without any task or reward. Surprisingly, 66% (2391/3601) of the MEC broad spiking neurons were significantly modulated by the bar position on the screen. Visual tuning in MEC had a pronounced dorsoventral topography --the tuning strength dropped from 79% in the dorsal most quartile to 40% in the ventral most quartile. Unlike major differences in spatial and other codes between MEC and LEC during free foraging experiments, LEC cells showed very similar visual tuning (392/606, 65%), including the dorso-ventral gradient in LEC5. Additionally, the majority of putative interneurons, from MEC as well as LEC, showed similar, widespread visual tuning, unlike spatial tasks. Neurons also encoded the object motion direction (naso-temporal vs. temporo-nasal visual motion) with changes in mean rate, tuning strength and/or tuning location. Such directional nature of visual tuning indicates significant history-dependence or sequence encoding. Consistently, replacing the continuous motion by randomly flashing bar of light abolished bar-tuning in two-thirds of continuous bar-tuned cells and substantially altered tuning in the rest. These results reveal the contribution of purely visual inputs in generating anatomically organized responses in the majority of entorhinal neurons. The prevalence and similarity of visual tuning across all layers of MEC as well as LEC exceeds that of other known functional cell types (like grid cells in MEC or egocentric object tuning/time-cells in LEC) during spatial navigation tasks and could be foundational in understanding entorhinal complexity.

Article.Title: Sex Differences in Human Subcortical Anatomy are Robust and Replicable in Adulthood, Already Evident Prepubertally, and Aligned with Sex Chromosomal and Gonadal Influences
Article.Authors: Lee, H. M.; Liu, S.; Lalonde, F.; Clasen, L.; Guma, E.; DeCasien, A.; Moraczewski, D.; Thomas, A. G.; Lerch, J. P.; Devenyi, G. A.; Chakravarty, M.; Berman, K. F.; Delaney, A.; Raznahan, A.
Article.Abstract: The existence and mechanistic bases of sex effects on human subcortical anatomy remain unclear. To address these gaps, we combined structural neuroimaging of sex differences in subcortical volume and shape across three independent cohorts (combined N=2,886) with neuroimaging maps of sex chromosomal and endocrine effects from three clinical cohorts (combined N=313, including sex chromosome aneuploidies and isolated gonadotropin-releasing hormone deficiency).
