Article.Abstract: Oxidative stress is widely recognized as a key mechanism involved in the onset and progression of numerous human diseases [...]

Article.Title: Integrative Bioinformatics Analysis Incorporating Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Identifies Putative Pathogenic HNF1B Missense Variants Associated with HNF1B-MODY
Article.Authors: Aldharee H.
Article.Abstract: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5 (MODY5 or HNF1B-MODY) is a rare form of diabetes caused by variants in HNF1B. Patients with MODY5 exhibit high blood sugar levels and symptoms commonly associated with both type 1 and type 2 diabetes (T1D, T2D), along with kidney and pancreatic issues. Nonetheless, diagnosis, treatment and management approaches depend on specific genotype–phenotype associations. Interpretation of HNF1B missense variants remains challenging because of conflicting classifications and limited clinical evidence. This study aimed to improve the interpretation of HNF1B missense variants with conflicting evidence regarding pathogenicity and thereby advance the genetic and molecular understanding of HNF1B-MODY. An integrative computational approach combining artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and conventional bioinformatic tools, including Panther, SIFT, SNAP2, Meta-SNP, PhD-SNP, PolyPhen-2, and AlphaMissense, was used to identify deleterious missense variants in the HNF1B gene. The variants were further processed to determine their effects on protein conformation, stability, function, and conservation across species. Among 982 reported variants retrieved from the ClinVar database, 368 were classified as missense. Only 47 missense variants were labelled with conflicting classification and reported with clinical uncertainty. Consensus analysis by all tools identified five candidate variants (His153Arg, Asn298Asp, Arg303His, Lys305Glu, and Val458Gly), representing 10.6% (5/47) as potentially pathogenic. AlphaMissense classified all five as likely pathogenic, with scores ranging from 0.8921 to 1.000. Secondary structure analysis indicates that the His153Arg, Asn298Asp, Arg303His, and Lys305Glu variants are in the helical region, while the Val458Gly variant is located within the coil region. Interestingly, all five filtered variants are predicted by the I-Mutant and MuPro tools to reduce protein stability. The three-dimensional (3D) protein structures were constructed using the Deep Learning-Based Iterative Threading Assembly Refinement (D-I-TASSER) tool and visualised by UCSF Chimera. Structural modelling showed similarity between the mutant and wild-type models, with RMSD values ranging from 0.77 to 1.36 Å. The multiple sequence alignments show that amino acids at variant sites across all variants are highly conserved among species. These findings show that combining traditional bioinformatics with artificial intelligence and machine learning improves the interpretation of HNF1B missense variants with clinical uncertainty. Integrating computational predictions with structural, evolutionary, and clinical data provides a framework for prioritising variants for further functional and clinical investigation.

Article.Title: Methylsulfonylmethane as a Bioactive Nutraceutical: Molecular Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence, Combination Therapy, Dosing, and Safety
Article.Authors: Yoon Y.; Hwang J.; Kim J.; Lee J.; Kim S.; Kim Y.; Lam K.
Article.Abstract: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM; dimethyl sulfone) is an organosulfur nutraceutical used primarily for joint symptoms, although its molecular actions and clinical applicability beyond osteoarthritis remain uncertain. This narrative review integrates pharmacological, preclinical, and human evidence on MSM, with emphasis on musculoskeletal disorders, multi-ingredient formulations, dosing, safety, toxicology, and clinical monitoring. Experimental studies implicate NF-κB and NLRP3 signaling, redox regulation, sulfur metabolism, and AMPK/mTOR/ULK1-related autophagy; however, most pathway-level evidence remains preclinical. Human clinical evidence is comparatively most developed for knee osteoarthritis, although it remains limited to small, short-term randomized trials reporting modest symptomatic improvement rather than established structural or disease-modifying benefit. Recent evidence syntheses also identify signals for glucosamine–MSM and glucosamine–chondroitin–MSM combinations, although certainty is limited and the independent contribution of MSM cannot be determined. Tendon studies largely evaluate multi-ingredient products, preventing attribution of benefit to MSM alone. Evidence in cardiometabolic disease, gastrointestinal health, exercise recovery, and toxicant exposure is preliminary. MSM is not a direct metal chelator and should not replace established chelation therapy. Short-term studies have used approximately 1–6 g/day with generally mild gastrointestinal adverse effects, whereas long-term safety, formal drug-interaction data, and clinically validated biomarker-guided dosing remain undefined. MSM should therefore be considered an adjunct with indication-dependent evidence rather than a broadly applicable anti-inflammatory or detoxification supplement.

Article.Title: Reversibility of Male Factor Infertility: Mechanisms and Evidence from the Literature
Article.Authors: La Vignera S.; Calogero A.; Cannarella R.; Crafa A.; Barbagallo F.; Condorelli R.
Article.Abstract: Male factor infertility contributes to approximately 50% of reproductive failure in couples worldwide. We conducted a narrative critical review synthesizing evidence from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, and clinical practice guidelines on reversible and irreversible causes of male infertility, examining hormonal, surgical, pharmacological, lifestyle, and drug-induced etiologies. The majority of identifiable etiologies demonstrate some degree of reversibility. Varicocele (prevalence 25–40% in infertile men) achieves natural pregnancy rates of 30–40% after varicocelectomy. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism responds to gonadotropin therapy with spermatogenesis induction in 90–95% of cases. Obstructive azoospermia achieves ductal patency rates of 85–97% with microsurgical reconstruction. Male accessory gland inflammation is reversible with prompt antibiotic therapy. Spermiotoxic drug exposures—including anabolic-androgenic steroids, sulfasalazine, and chemotherapy—show variable reversibility depending on agent and duration of exposure. Normogonadotropic normotestosteronemic oligozoospermia represents a commonly encountered phenotype that may respond to empirical medical therapy. Lifestyle modifications demonstrate measurable benefits in selected patients. Irreversible causes include Klinefelter syndrome, Y-chromosome AZFa/b microdeletions, and severe post-chemotherapy damage. Systematic andrological evaluation, including comprehensive drug history, is essential to identify treatable causes and guide clinical management.

Article.Title: The Effect of Fosinopril on Achilles Tendon Healing in a Rat Model
Article.Authors: Asar Ş.; Balık M.; Tümkaya L.; Mercantepe T.; Topçu A.; Şahin R.
Article.Abstract: In addition to their antihypertensive effects, angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors possess endothelial protective properties. It has been shown that ACE inhibitors reduce fibrosis and adhesion during the tendon healing process by suppressing angiotensin II. In this experimental study, we aimed to investigate the effect of fosinopril, a commonly used ACE inhibitor in the treatment of hypertension, on Achilles tendon healing in rats. A total of 80 Sprague–Dawley rats were used and divided into four groups: healthy control group (Group 1), Achilles tendon rupture and repair group (Group 2), Achilles tendon rupture and repair with fosinopril administration (Group 3), and healthy rats treated with fosinopril only (Group 4). At the end of the experiment, rats were sacrificed at the 1st, 2nd, and 4th weeks, and the groups were compared using biochemical and histological methods. For statistical analysis, data distribution was assessed for normality. Group comparisons were conducted using one-way ANOVA or the Kruskal–Wallis test as appropriate, followed by post hoc pairwise comparisons with correction for multiple testing. According to the biochemical analysis, the levels of TBARS (a marker of oxidative stress) were significantly lower, and total thiol levels (an antioxidant marker) were significantly higher in the fosinopril-treated groups compared to those without fosinopril treatment. In histopathological evaluations using a damage scoring system for edema, hemorrhage, and inflammation, scores were lower in the fosinopril-treated groups. Immunohistochemical analyses revealed that the expression levels of VEGF, collagen I, and collagen III were lower in the fosinopril-treated groups compared to the untreated groups at the same time points. This study demonstrates that fosinopril exerts antioxidant effects during the Achilles tendon healing process and provides favorable histopathological findings during the evaluated period of tendon healing.

Article.Title: Modulation of FOXO3 Transcriptional Regulation by Cisplatin and Curcumin in Human Embryonic Kidney Cells
Article.Authors: Coronado-Moreno E.; Mendoza-Santos V.; Larre I.; González-Cázares D.; Dorantes E.; Medina-Contreras O.; Sánchez-Boiso A.; Rodriguez-Espino B.; Guadarrama O.; Medeiros M.
Article.Abstract: Cisplatin is a highly effective anti-neoplastic agent, but its clinical application is limited by its association with severe nephrotoxicity. Although extensive research has identified several mechanisms underlying cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity, the precise molecular pathways remain incompletely understood. Recent studies have highlighted the role of intrinsic survival, senescence, and longevity signaling pathways, including those governed by the FOXO3 transcription factor. In this study, we examined the effects of cisplatin and curcumin on the DNA methylation status and mRNA expression of FOXO3 in human embryonic kidney (HEK293) cells. Our results indicate that the FOXO3 promoter is methylated in cisplatin-treated cells, and that cisplatin regulates FOXO3 transcription in a dose-dependent manner. Quantitative RT-qPCR revealed that moderate cytotoxic concentrations of cisplatin (10 and 40 µM) significantly downregulate FOXO3 mRNA. Furthermore, co-treatment with the antioxidant curcumin successfully restored and enhanced FOXO3 expression at moderate cisplatin doses (10 µM) but failed to rescue expression at high doses (40 µM). Moreover, curcumin treatment (10 µM) reverses the effects of low-dose, but not high-dose, cisplatin (40 and 60 µM). Taken together, these findings provide a foundation for understanding the epigenetic and transcriptional regulation of FOXO3 and highlight its potential as a target for antioxidant-mediated nephroprotection and its role in cell survival.

Article.Title: Feasibility Study of an Assay Measuring Activity of Oral Cancer Protease Mixtures to Cleave Protease-Activated Receptor 2, an Oral Cancer Pain Mediator
Article.Authors: Ramirez-Garcia P.; Dolgalev I.; Zubli S.; Schmidt B.; Albertson D.
Article.Abstract: Oral cancer patients suffer pain that is patient-specific and heterogeneous at the site of the tumor. Protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR2), a G-protein coupled receptor and an oral cancer mediator, is activated by protease cleavage of an N-terminal ligand. Once cleaved, the receptor is retained at the plasma membrane or re-distributed (trafficking) to internal sites followed by downstream protease-specific signaling. The oral cancer tumor microenvironment (TME) is replete with protases that activate PAR2, potentially evoking PAR2 trafficking and signaling that is unique to each cancer and reflecting the protease composition of the individual TMEs. To measure PAR2 cleavage activity in oral cancer samples, an array of overlapping peptides spanning the PAR2 N-terminus was assembled. In this feasibility study, we assayed the cleavage activity of individual PAR2-activating proteases and mixtures of proteases modeling the oral cancer TME. Additionally, we confirmed that PAR2-cleaving proteases are active in oral cancer patient saliva, a sample that can be collected non-invasively to measure PAR2 cleavage in patients when they are experiencing pain prior to surgery. Further studies should elucidate the utility of the peptide array to measure PAR2-activating proteolysis in cancer samples.

Article.Title: Ferroptosis Susceptibility in Pediatric Immune Thrombocytopenia: Alteration in Mesenchymal Stromal Cells
Article.Authors: Di Feo G.; Marrapodi M.; Di Domenico O.; Argenziano L.; La Manna M.; Lembo E.; Palumbo G.; Rossi F.; Di Paola A.
Article.Abstract: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is the most common pediatric thrombocytopenia, characterized by immune-mediated platelet destruction and altered inflammatory responses. Among these alterations, mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) from ITP patients display reduced viability and impaired immunoregulatory functions. Our previous work revealed dysregulated iron metabolism in ITP-MSCs, with increased intracellular iron accumulation driven by hepcidin–FPN1 axis disruption and overexpression of iron importers. Given the link between iron overload, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis, a regulated iron-dependent form of cell death, we investigated whether ITP-MSCs exhibit oxidative and molecular alterations associated with ferroptosis. ITP-MSCs showed increased ROS levels and ACSL4 expression, together with reduced expression of proteins involved in ferroptosis-related antioxidant defense, including SLC3A2, SLC7A11, and GPX4. Increased extracellular release of HMGB1, a DAMP associated with cellular stress and different forms of regulated cell death, was also observed. Treatment with Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) and Deferasirox (DFX) reduced oxidative stress and partially restored the expression of ferroptosis-related markers. Similarly, high-dose dexamethasone (HD-Dexa) reduced ROS and ACSL4 levels and limited extracellular HMGB1 release. Collectively, these findings support increased susceptibility to ferroptotic stress in ITP-MSCs and reveal a ferroptosis-associated oxidative stress phenotype with concomitant alterations in ferroptosis-related molecular pathways. Moreover, the effects of HD-Dexa, DFX, and Fer-1 suggest that modulation of these pathways may represent a potential strategy for limiting oxidative cellular damage in ITP-MSCs.

Article.Title: Molecular Biomarkers Linking Psoriasis and Cardiovascular Disease: Current Evidence and Clinical Perspectives
Article.Authors: Matwiejuk M.; Myśliwiec H.; Mikłosz A.; Jarocewicz O.; Chabowski A.; Flisiak I.
Article.Abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disease affecting the skin, nails, and joints. Its complex pathogenesis results from interactions between genetic susceptibility and environmental factors and is accompanied by an increased risk of multiple systemic comorbidities, particularly cardiovascular disease. Growing evidence indicates that both conditions share common molecular pathways driven by chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, metabolic disturbances, and immune dysregulation. Among the emerging molecular biomarkers, chemerin, endocan, and growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15) have attracted considerable attention due to their role in vascular homeostasis, adipose tissue biology, glucose metabolism, and inflammatory signaling. This review summarizes current evidence on the involvement of these biomarkers in psoriasis and cardiovascular disease, highlighting their contribution to the molecular mechanisms underlying the psoriasis–cardiovascular disease axis. Furthermore, we discussed their potential usefulness as candidate biomarkers for cardiovascular risk. However, prospective validation is strictly required to confirm their clinical utility and establish their incremental predictive value beyond conventional risk factors.

Article.Title: Preoperative Serum Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) Levels in Class III Obesity: A Prospective Controlled Observational Study
Article.Authors: Kutluer N.; Ağ O.; Gündoğdu T.; Öğüt M.; Kılıç D.; Ayyıldız H.; Doğan S.; Bozan M.
Article.Abstract: Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) is a membrane cation channel activated by oxidative stress products that are chronically elevated in class III obesity. Although tissue-level TRPA1 biology is increasingly well described, the biological meaning of circulating immunoreactive TRPA1 remains poorly established. This single-centre, prospective, controlled observational study compared preoperative serum TRPA1 between adults with class III obesity scheduled for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy and contemporaneous controls, and explored metabolic and inflammatory correlates of the circulating signal. Serum TRPA1 was quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) in 42 consecutive surgical candidates and 36 controls. The primary analysis used continuous (log-transformed) TRPA1 with age- and sex-adjusted logistic regression; ROC-derived dichotomisation was retained only as an exploratory analysis. Serum TRPA1 did not differ between groups (median 309.8 vs. 340.5 pg/mL; Mann–Whitney U, p = 0.323; Hodges–Lehmann median difference [obesity − control] −30.8 pg/mL, bootstrap 95% CI −227.43 to 43.02). After adjustment for age and sex, continuous log-TRPA1 was not independently associated with obesity status (OR per log-unit 0.88, 95% CI 0.46–1.69; p = 0.699), and discrimination was poor (AUC 0.435; 95% CI 0.305–0.562). Established inflammatory and metabolic markers differed between groups, but serum TRPA1 did not track them. In this cohort, preoperative serum TRPA1 did not distinguish class III obesity from controls. The negative circulating finding should be interpreted as lack of evidence for a large between-group difference in ELISA-measured serum TRPA1—and as a potential translational disconnect from tissue TRPA1 biology—rather than as the definitive exclusion of any tissue-level role for the channel.

Article.Title: Sugar-Specific Modulation of Trophoblast Function and Bioenergetics Under Metabolic Stress Conditions
Article.Authors: Thurmond E.; Boyer M.; Bikman B.; Reynolds P.; Arroyo J.
Article.Abstract: How sugars other than glucose affect trophoblast function is poorly understood, particularly under the metabolic stress of diabetic pregnancy. We compared glucose, fructose, and the minimally metabolized sugar allulose in two trophoblast cell lines, SW71 (first-trimester, extravillous-like) and BeWo (choriocarcinoma-derived, villous). Each sugar was added at 25 mM for 24 h to the cells’ standard glucose-containing media (11 mM, SW71; 17.5 mM, BeWo) to model metabolic stress. All three sugars increased the number of cells recovered (2.4- to 6.5-fold in SW71; ~10- to 15-fold in BeWo) and reduced viability (~9–75%), with fructose causing the largest loss in both lines. Intracellular reactive oxygen species increased 5.2- to 7.8-fold with all sugars. Oxygen consumption differed by sugar: in SW71 cells, glucose and allulose increased ADP-stimulated and succinate-supported respiration, whereas fructose reduced it, and in BeWo cells only fructose increased it. SW71 invasion was ~7-fold higher after allulose than after glucose or fructose. BeWo cells were studied undifferentiated, so effects on syncytialization were not assessed. The three sugars are therefore not interchangeable in their effects on trophoblast cells in vitro. Because the concentrations exceed those in maternal blood, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require testing at physiological concentrations and in primary trophoblast models.

Article.Title: Mito–Nuclear Interactions in Livestock: Implications for Adaptation, Productivity, and Precision Breeding
Article.Authors: Panigrahi M.; Rajawat D.; Upadhyay A.; Devadharshini K.; Ranjith G.; Rath P.; Verma S.; Nayak S.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondria are central regulators of cellular energy metabolism, stress responses, and physiological adaptation, with their functions depending on the coordinated interaction between mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and nuclear DNA (nDNA). These mito–nuclear interactions are essential for maintaining oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), cellular homeostasis, and overall organismal fitness. Increasing evidence suggests that mito–nuclear compatibility influences a wide range of economically important traits in livestock, including growth, milk production, reproduction, feed efficiency, disease resistance, and environmental adaptation. This review provides a comprehensive overview of mitochondrial and nuclear genome organization, mechanisms of mito–nuclear communication, and their biological significance in livestock species. Key mechanisms discussed include mito–nuclear co-evolution, anterograde and retrograde signaling, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated signaling, epigenetic regulation, mitophagy, mitochondrial biogenesis, and mito–nuclear incompatibility. The review further highlights the role of mito–nuclear interactions in adaptation to heat stress, high-altitude environments, metabolic challenges, and disease resistance, as well as their influence on productivity traits such as milk yield, growth performance, fertility, reproductive efficiency, and longevity. Advances in genomic and multi-omics technologies, including genome-wide association studies (GWAS), mitogenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, network biology, and systems genomics, have greatly enhanced our understanding of mitochondrial function and its contribution to complex traits. Furthermore, integrating mitochondrial information into genomic selection, marker-assisted breeding, climate-smart livestock improvement, and precision livestock farming (PLF) offers new opportunities to enhance productivity, resilience, and sustainability. Understanding the genetic and functional basis of mito–nuclear interactions will facilitate the development of next-generation precision breeding strategies aimed at improving livestock performance under changing environmental conditions.

Article.Title: Epitalon and Epithalamin: A Narrative Review of Mechanistic, Preclinical, and Clinical Evidence
Article.Authors: Jain A.; Gallacher D.; Issa M.; Deer T.; Yong R.; Diwan S.; Lee W.; Sayed D.; Amirdelfan K.; Robinson C.
Article.Abstract: Epitalon (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) is a synthetic tetrapeptide developed from the amino-acid composition of epithalamin, a chemically distinct pineal-derived polypeptide preparation. This narrative review evaluates the mechanistic, preclinical, and human evidence for synthetic epitalon in the context of regenerative and longevity medicine, while considering epithalamin studies separately as historical context. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched through 22 September 2026, with primary experimental and clinical studies prioritized and evidence appraised by study design, model, sample size, intervention, outcomes, safety reporting, and independent replication. Epitalon has been reported to modulate telomere-maintenance pathways, circadian and neuroendocrine function, oxidative stress, and cellular aging markers. Preclinical studies suggest biological activity, but direct evidence in musculoskeletal disease models is lacking. Human evidence is limited to small physiological or biomarker studies and an older controlled study in retinitis pigmentosa; no adequately powered randomized trial has established therapeutic efficacy. Pharmacokinetic, dose-ranging, and long-term safety data remain inadequate, while oncologic, immunogenicity, product-quality, and regulatory uncertainties following a 2026 FDA advisory review remain unresolved. Epitalon is therefore biologically active but clinically unproven, and further standardized pharmacologic, safety, and disease-specific studies are needed before clinical translation.

Article.Title: Production, Optimization and Characterization of Biobased Itaconic Acid from Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Article.Authors: Velioglu Tosuner Z.; Kosaca M.; Ozturk Urek R.; Yilmaz O.; Yilmaz C.
Article.Abstract: Itaconic acid (IA) is an important bio-based platform chemical with applications in the production of polymers, coatings, resins, and other value-added materials. However, its conventional microbial production relies predominantly on microorganisms that present safety and process-related limitations. This study investigated Saccharomyces cerevisiae BY4742 as a potentially safer microbial platform for the production of bio-based IA under submerged fermentation conditions. IA production was optimized using response surface methodology with a Box–Behnken design, considering glucose concentration, initial pH, and CaCI2 concentration as independent variables. The maximum IA concentration of 1133.50 ± 54.92 mg/L was obtained at 30 °C, pH 4.5, with 10% (w/v) glucose and without CaCI2 supplementation after 216 h of fermentation. The fermentation-derived IA was subsequently recovered and characterized using high-performance liquid chromatography, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, 1H-nuclear magnetic resonance (1H-NMR), and thermogravimetric analysis. The analytical results confirmed the molecular identity and high chromatographic purity of the recovered IA. Furthermore, the homopolymerization ability of the fermentation-derived IA was evaluated and compared with that of commercial IA under the same reaction conditions. The 1H-NMR results demonstrated changes consistent with consumption of the IA C=C double bond following polymerization, indicating that the fermentation-derived IA retained its ability to undergo homopolymerization. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of S. cerevisiae for producing structurally confirmed bio-based IA and provide a proof of concept for its use as a renewable monomer for poly(itaconic acid) synthesis, supporting its further investigation for the development of bio-based polymeric materials.

Article.Title: Structure, Evolution and Functional Inference on the CDP Gene Family in European Hazelnut
Article.Authors: Amoroso C.; Auzino B.; Evangelista A.; Pilolli R.; Nitride C.; Andolfo G.
Article.Abstract: Food allergy is an IgE-mediated response of the immune system of sensitive subjects to specific proteins. The recent WHO/FAO consultation included hazelnut (Corylus avellana L.) in the list of global priority allergenic ingredients. One of the most common hazelnut allergen groups encompasses the Cupin_1 domain-containing proteins (CDPs). To date, three CDP allergens (Cor a 9, Cor a 11, and Cor a 16) have been deposited into the official WHO/IUIS database. Recently, using a whole-genome approach, the Cor a loci were mapped in four Corylus species. However, the task of identifying novel CDP allergen candidates directly within the genome has not yet been addressed. The recently available C. avellana cv. ‘Tombul’ genome sequence allowed the identification of 114 hazelnut CDP-encoding genes. The maximum likelihood analysis allowed us to reconstruct the evolutionary relationships underlying the diversification and expansion of the CDP superfamily. Several duplication events associated with lineage-specific evolution were discovered. Interestingly, conserved epitopes and amino acid motifs that likely play a role in allergenic function were also identified. A total of 42 cis-acting regulatory elements were shared in the promoter regions of known and new putative allergens. Using the well-known CDP allergens as an internal benchmark, we have identified and molecularly analyzed new CDP allergen candidates. To provide a first transcriptional characterization, Cor a 9, Cor a 11, and Cor a 16 were analyzed by real-time PCR. The expression analysis showed generally low relative transcript levels of Cor a genes in immature reproductive tissues compared with young leaves. Interestingly, mass spectrometry analysis confirmed the accumulation of known allergens and several predicted CDP allergen candidates in commercial hazelnut flour. The data reported here may help to further address food safety questions and could be conveniently used in breeding research aimed at developing hypoallergenic cultivars.

Article.Title: Untargeted Metabolomics Reveals Regional and Cultivar-Associated Metabolomic Variation in Soybeans Across Northeast China
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Gou L.; You H.; Wang F.; Zhu J.; Wang Y.; Xia Z.; Kuan Z.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Soybean (Glycine max) quality and metabolic composition are shaped by complex interactions between genetic background and agro-ecological conditions, making metabolic characterization across major production regions valuable for germplasm evaluation and quality-oriented breeding. In this study, an untargeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics approach was applied to compare the mature seed metabolomes of nine representative commercial soybean cultivars sampled from two major production regions in Northeast China: Heilongjiang (HLJ, four cultivars from Harbin) and Liaoning (LN, five cultivars from Shenyang). Because region-specific cultivars were collected from a single site and seed lot per province without direct site-level meteorological or soil measurements, genotype and environment are confounded in this observational design, and the observed differences reflect the combined variation in the sampled cultivar–location cohorts. After preprocessing, 8283 features were putatively annotated (MSI Level 2/3). Multivariate statistical analyses (PCA, PLS-DA, and OPLS-DA) combined with cultivar-grouped cross-validation revealed clear metabolic separation between the sampled HLJ and LN cohorts. A total of 1485 putatively annotated metabolites (VIP > 1.0, subsample-level FDR < 0.05, fold change HLJ/LN > 2.0 or <0.5) were screened as exploratory candidate differential metabolites, with 953 exhibiting higher abundance (FC>2.0) and 532 exhibiting lower abundance (FC<0.5, i.e., higher abundance in LN) in HLJ soybeans relative to LN soybeans. Exploratory KEGG pathway mapping (based on nominal p-values, as no pathway reached FDR-adjusted q<0.05) indicated nominal enrichment in isoflavonoid biosynthesis (p=0.0043, q=0.261) and tryptophan metabolism (p=0.0093, q=0.283); specifically, sampled LN cultivar–location combinations exhibited higher steady-state abundances of isoflavones and their glycosylated derivatives, whereas sampled HLJ soybeans exhibited higher steady-state abundances of specific lipid species (unsaturated fatty acyls, sphingolipids) and tryptophan-derived indoleamines. In the absence of direct environmental measurements, potential links between these steady-state metabolic signatures and regional macroclimatic differences (such as thermal regimes or high-latitude cold stress) are proposed strictly as exploratory, literature-informed hypotheses. Overall, these findings provide preliminary candidate metabolic markers for characterizing the sampled regional soybean germplasm; however, independent validation across additional harvest years, multiple geographic sites, independent seed lots, and broader cultivar panels will be required before these candidate metabolites can be considered validated biomarkers for geographic authentication.

Article.Title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Network Analysis Identifies Candidate Kinase-Mediated Thyroid-Associated Targets of Withaferin A
Article.Authors: Abdullah E.; Alameen A.; AlAfaleq N.; Alharbi M.
Article.Abstract: Withaferin A (WA), a bioactive steroidal lactone derived from Withania somnifera, has been reported to exhibit diverse pharmacological activities, including anti-inflammatory and metabolic regulatory effects. Although previous studies suggest a potential link between WA and thyroid-related molecular pathways, the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Here, we employed a comprehensive computational approach to explore WA-responsive molecular changes potentially relevant to thyroid-associated processes. RNA-sequencing data from WA-treated MCF-10A human mammary epithelial cells (GSE158085) were analysed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Because thyroid-specific WA transcriptomic datasets are not currently available, the DEGs were intersected with curated hypothyroidism-associated genes to generate a cross-tissue, exploratory set of candidate genes. The genes that overlapped were used to construct protein–protein interaction networks, prioritize high-centrality candidate genes, and conduct enrichment analyses for transcription factors and kinases. Further analysis of selected upstream kinases was performed using molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations with WA. A total of 1458 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, 10 of which overlapped with hypothyroidism-associated genes. Network analysis identified candidate interactions among the overlapping genes, while higher-confidence analysis retained four connected genes (PTPN22, STAT4, DUOX2, and DUOXA2). Transcription factor enrichment identified ERG, SUZ12, NANOG, TCF3, RUNX1, and TP63 as potential upstream regulators, while kinase enrichment identified candidate upstream kinases associated with the predicted regulatory network. Based on enrichment evidence, structural availability, and literature-supported biological relevance, MAPK14 (p38α), AKT1, and MAPK8 (JNK1) were selected for molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. Structural analyses suggested potential interactions between WA and the selected kinases, with target-specific dynamic behaviour across the simulated systems. Collectively, the findings highlight WA-responsive genes and predicted gene–TF–kinase relationships that may be relevant to thyroid-associated molecular processes. However, these associations are hypothesis-generating and provide a basis for further investigation in thyroid-derived experimental models.

Article.Title: Waterpipe Smoke Condensate Impairs p53 Nuclear Localization in Association with HIF-1α Stabilization
Article.Authors: Nawafleh H.; Thiery J.; Elsayed Y.; Abdou A.; Chouaib S.; Zaarour R.
Article.Abstract: Waterpipe (shisha or hookah) smoking is recognized as a risk factor for lung cancer; however, its interference with hypoxia stress and tumor suppressor pathways in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is poorly defined. In this study, NSCLC cell lines (A549, H460, H226 with endogenous wild-type p53, and H1299 transiently expressing wild-type or p53 mutants) were exposed to waterpipe smoke condensate (WPSC) under normoxic and/or hypoxic conditions. WPSC induced HIF-1α stabilization under normoxic conditions, accompanied by predominantly cytoplasmic localization and without corresponding induction of the canonical HIF-1 target genes examined. In parallel, WPSC transiently reduced nuclear p53 localization without altering total p53 protein levels. In A549 cells, WPSC pretreatment attenuated irradiation-induced expression of the p53 target genes cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1A (CDKN1A) and BTG anti-proliferation factor 2 (BTG2). Pharmacological inhibition of HIF-1α partially restored nuclear p53 localization, supporting the involvement of HIF-1α in this response. Co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated an association between HIF-1α and p53 following WPSC exposure. Collectively, these findings show that WPSC-induced HIF-1α stabilization under normoxic conditions is associated with transient alterations in p53 localization and transcriptional response, supporting an involvement of HIF-1α in this process.

Article.Title: Nanoparticle-Enabled Immune-Dose Shaping in Breast Cancer Radiotherapy: Reconciling Tumor Immunogenicity with Systemic Immune Preservation
Article.Authors: Lunca S.; Morarasu S.; Dimofte G.
Article.Abstract: Radiotherapy can simultaneously promote tumor immunogenicity and damage the systemic immune compartments required to sustain antitumor responses. In breast cancer, radiation-induced lymphopenia is influenced by treatment geometry, irradiated volume, low-dose exposure, marrow and lymphoid irradiation, fractionation, and delivery characteristics, while nanoparticle radioenhancement can amplify tumor response through physical, redox, DNA-repair, and immune mechanisms. This hypothesis-driven translational review examines whether nanoparticle-generated biological amplification could be redirected from tumor intensification toward immune-dose shaping while preserving tumor control and immunogenicity. The evidence supports seven interacting dimensions of potential exchange: physical dose, volume/spatial exposure, distributed low-dose exposure, marrow dose, geometry/modality, fractionation, and temporal/delivery exposure. Formal nanoparticle-enabled dose exchange remains limited, with the clearest breast-specific evidence confined to in vitro isoeffect analysis; no study has yet demonstrated preserved tumor isoeffect and immunogenicity together with reduced multicompartment immune injury after nanoparticle-enabled exposure reduction. We, therefore, propose a dual-endpoint framework integrating tumor control, immunogenicity, multicompartment immune preservation, dosimetry, and nanoparticle biodistribution, together with a staged translational pathway from quantitative preclinical exchange studies to comparative clinical testing. This strategy remains hypothesis-generating, with triple-negative breast cancer representing a particularly informative initial setting.

Article.Title: LGH-Transformer: A Hybrid CNN–Transformer Model for Multi-Class Bladder Tissue Classification from Cystoscopic Images
Article.Authors: Kurt H.; Kılıçarslan S.; Çiçekliyurt M.; Kiliçarslan S.
Article.Abstract: Automated analysis of cystoscopic images may support consistent characterization of bladder tissue patterns, but reported performance is highly sensitive to patient composition, data partitioning, and evaluation methodology. Objective: This study provides an exploratory comparison of convolutional neural networks, Transformer-based models, and a proposed Local–Global Hybrid Transformer (LGH-Transformer) for four-class bladder tissue image classification. The dataset comprised 1754 frames and used the publicly released 1257/308/189 training–validation–held-out test split. The annotation-defined held-out test composition was HGC = 74, LGC = 53, NST = 37, and NTL = 25 (n = 189). Images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels, normalized, and augmented only in the training subset. Adam and RMSprop were evaluated. Accuracy and macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score were calculated from the integer-count evaluation matrices. The highest held-out accuracy, 187/189 (0.9894), was reached by seven model–optimizer configurations: DenseNet201–RMSprop, XCiT Medium 24 P16–Adam, ConvNeXt Base–Adam, CoAtNet–Adam, ConvNeXt Base–RMSprop, CoAtNet–RMSprop, and the proposed LGH-Transformer–RMSprop; MobileNet–Adam and Xcep-tion–RMSprop each yielded 185/189 (0.9788), and LGH-Transformer–Adam yielded 186/189 (0.9841). On a 189-frame test set, differences in one to two frames do not establish statistical superiority, so these configurations are reported as a top-accuracy tier rather than as a ranked superiority claim. Within this tier, the LGH-Transformer had the smallest computational footprint (≈18.2 M parameters and ≈4.1 GFLOPs, versus 20.0–88.6 M parameters and 4.3–16.2 GFLOPs for the other top-tier models). Component-wise ablation experiments showed accuracy decreases of 0.0106, 0.0053, and 0.0053 after removing the CNN tokenizer, local attention, and global attention, respectively. The LGH-Transformer reaches the top accuracy tier of this 18-architecture benchmark at the lowest parameter and FLOP budget within that tier, supporting an internally consistent, efficiency-oriented comparison within the available cohort. The absence of task-aligned external validation and the small number of held-out patients require the findings to be interpreted as exploratory internal validation rather than evidence of clinical generalizability.

Article.Title: Improving Grain Shape of the Rice Variety Exiangsimiao by Introgressing the Long-Grain Allele of GL7/GW7
Article.Authors: Hu H.; Qi Z.; Wang Z.; Liu N.; Xu J.; Liu H.; Yang L.; Jiang J.; Liang F.; Qiu X.
Article.Abstract: Exiangsimiao (EXSM) is a high-yield and high-quality indica variety and restorer line. However, its grains are not sufficiently slender. In this study, the long-grain allele of the grain shape gene GL7/GW7 was introgressed into EXSM via marker-assisted selection combined with backcross breeding, and two improved long-grain lines (EXSM-IL1 and EXSM-IL2) were developed. Their background recovery rates reached 96.70% and 97.50%, respectively. Their grain lengths (GLs) and length-to-width ratios (LWRs) were significantly higher than EXSM. The milling quality, especially the head milled rice rate (HMRR), of both improved lines was significantly lower than EXSM. EXSM-IL1 showed no significant difference in grain yield (GY) to EXSM, although both improved lines had shorter total growth duration (TGD), longer panicle length (PL), and a lower seed setting ratio (SSR) and 1000-grain weight (KGW). Six hybrid combinations derived from the improved lines exhibited longer GL, higher LWR and narrower GW than those of the hybrid combinations derived from EXSM. The TGD and KGW of the six hybrid combinations were significantly lower compared with the hybrids from EXSM. Furthermore, the two improved lines carried 41 favorable genes associated with crucial traits. These results provide the basis for rice grain shape improvement and supply long-grain and high-quality breeding lines and restorer lines for rice production in southern China.

Article.Title: Possible Links Between PM2.5-Induced NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation and Its Role in Lung Cancer Progression and Drug Resistance
Article.Authors: Worawichitchaikun T.; Wantanachaisaeng P.; Teeppaibul T.; Suwannalert P.
Article.Abstract: The rising incidence of lung cancer is increasingly linked to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure, highlighting its role as a risk factor of lung carcinogenesis. However, the molecular mechanisms behind PM2.5 and the disease remain incompletely understood. Exposure to PM2.5 triggers inflammatory processes, primarily via ROS overproduction, which activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, a cytosolic NOD-like pattern recognition receptor protein complex that cleaves caspase-1 and drives maturation of pro-interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and pro-interleukin-18 (IL-18), leading to chronic pulmonary inflammation. Based on current evidence, this review displays PM2.5-induced ROS upregulation as an essential trigger of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in lung cancer development and progression and hypothesises that the signalling of NLRP3 may contribute to molecular pathways associated with lung cancer drug resistance. There have been uses of NLRP3 inhibitors in clinical trials of different inflammatory diseases, but none has yet reached clinical testing in oncology. We propose the potential of NLRP3 as a possible prognostic marker and a therapeutic target for PM2.5-associated lung cancer drug resistance.

Article.Title: Changes in Isthmin-1, Irisin, and the AGE–RAGE Axis Following LSG: A Prospective Single-Center Cohort Study
Article.Authors: Kupczyk W.; Boinska J.; Słomka A.; Kupczyk K.; Jackowski M.; Żekanowska E.
Article.Abstract: This prospective single-center cohort study evaluated changes in serum levels of novel adipokines and myokines, including isthmin-1 and irisin, as well as the advanced glycation end product (AGE)–soluble receptor for AGE (sRAGE) axis and monomeric C-reactive protein (mCRP) in patients with obesity before and 5 months after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG). The study included 38 patients with obesity (26 females and 12 males) with a median age of 42 years who underwent LSG. Laboratory parameters were assessed using commercially available immunoenzymatic assays. We observed a significant decrease in isthmin-1 concentration at the postoperative time point (Me = 2.10 ng/mL vs. Me = 1.93 ng/mL, p = 0.009). Moreover, a significant increase in irisin levels (Me = 7.33 µg/mL vs. Me = 10.64 µg/mL, p = 0.002) and AGEs (Me = 589.50 ng/mL vs. Me = 698.60 ng/mL, p = 0.015) was observed after LSG. A significant increase in AGE levels was also noted after normalization to total protein (Me = 8.34 ng/mg protein vs. Me = 10.37 ng/mg protein, p = 0.027). sRAGE levels were similar at both time points. Five months after LSG, mCRP levels were significantly lower (Me = 1.99 ng/mL vs. Me = 1.55 ng/mL, p = 0.020). Exploratory correlation analyses identified potential associations between AGEs and isthmin-1 (R = 0.37) and between sRAGE and irisin (R = −0.31) preoperatively. Five months after LSG, potential associations were observed between AGEs and irisin (R = 0.38) and between sRAGE and mCRP (R = −0.37). Our findings indicate a decrease in circulating isthmin-1 and mCRP, together with an increase in irisin and AGE concentrations following LSG, suggesting changes in selected metabolic and tissue-related biomarkers after surgery. Further studies are needed to determine the mechanisms underlying these changes and to clarify their potential clinical significance.

Article.Title: CD180-Associated B-Cell Alterations in Type 1 Diabetes and the In Vitro Effects of Chlorogenic Acid: An Integrated Transcriptomic and Experimental Study
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Mijit A.; Han R.; Li M.; Wu Y.; Cheng L.
Article.Abstract: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is an autoimmune disease involving progressive loss of pancreatic β-cells. Although B cells have been implicated in T1DM progression, the molecular characteristics associated with disease-related B-cell states remain unclear. Here, we investigated B-cell-associated molecular alterations in T1DM and explored the potential immunomodulatory effects of a natural compound. Public T1DM transcriptomic datasets were analyzed using differential expression analysis, WGCNA, and machine-learning approaches. Single-cell RNA sequencing was used to characterize Cd180 expression across B-cell states. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were used to explore potential interactions between CD180 and candidate compounds, and an exploratory DARTS assay was performed to assess CGA-associated changes in CD180 proteolytic susceptibility. CD180 expression was examined in pancreatic tissues from vehicle- and MSA-2-treated NOD mice. The effects of chlorogenic acid (CGA) were evaluated in vitro by exposing B cells to CGA during inflammatory stimulation, followed by washing and co-culture with MIN6 cells in CGA-free medium. Integrated transcriptomic analysis identified four T1DM-associated genes (CD180, KCNJ2, STEAP4, and ZXDA), among which CD180 showed the strongest association with B-cell-related immune alterations. Single-cell analysis showed increased Cd180 expression in inflammatory B-cell states together with enrichment of antigen-presentation-related programs. An exploratory DARTS experiment with matched loading-control data suggested altered CD180 proteolytic susceptibility following CGA exposure, although independent reproducibility remains to be established. In vitro, CGA exposure during inflammatory stimulation was associated with reduced CD180 expression in B cells and improved MIN6 cell viability and insulin-secretory responses during subsequent co-culture in CGA-free medium. CD180 is associated with inflammatory B-cell alterations in T1DM and may represent a candidate molecular feature of B-cell dysregulation. CGA treatment was associated with changes in CD180 expression in activated B cells and improved β-cell functional outcomes in vitro. These findings support further investigation of the relationship between CGA and CD180; however, whether the effects of CGA are specifically mediated through CD180 requires further experimental validation.

Article.Title: Urinary DNA Methylation Profiling Identifies a Biologically Distinct Subgroup of Low-Grade Urothelial Carcinoma with High-Grade-Associated Features
Article.Authors: Andreu-Inglés M.; Onoiu A.; Grifoll-Escoda M.; Hernández-Aguilera A.; Gumà-Padró J.; Riu F.; Peña K.; Camps J.; Parada D.
Article.Abstract: Bladder cancer surveillance remains challenging because conventional methods do not fully capture the biological heterogeneity within histologically low-grade urothelial carcinoma (LGUC). We evaluated whether urinary DNA methylation profiling using Bladder EpiCheck™ can identify clinically relevant LGUC subgroups in a retrospective single-center cohort of 134 patients with paired histopathology, urine cytology, and methylation results. Methylation positivity increased across negative histopathology, LGUC, and high-grade urothelial carcinoma (HGUC) (18.4%, 51.4%, and 91.5%, respectively). Within LGUC, 19 of 37 tumors (51.4%) were methylation-positive. Their EpiScores overlapped those of HGUC, whereas methylation-negative LGUCs exhibited scores similar to negative histopathology. Gaussian mixture modeling independently supported a bimodal distribution. Methylation-positive LGUCs demonstrated a higher Ki67 labeling index, more frequent MTAP loss (33.3% vs. 11.8%), and more recurrences, including recurrence as HGUC, than methylation-negative LGUCs. Conventional nuclear morphometry did not distinguish between the two LGUC subgroups. These exploratory findings suggest that urinary DNA methylation may identify a biologically distinct subset of histologically low-grade tumors with selected high-grade-associated features. Prospective external validation is required before methylation status can inform surveillance or treatment decisions.

Article.Title: Intraosseous Lidocaine Trigger Point Injection for Vertebrogenic Pain: From Molecular Principles to Clinical Applications: A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Al-Zamil M.; Shnayder N.; Petrova M.; Naprienko M.; Zhelambekov I.; Goncharova O.; Garganeeva N.; Kuleshova S.; Eremina O.; Dobrosmyslova A.
Article.Abstract: Intraosseous lidocaine trigger point injection (LTPI) has been utilized for an extended period in the management of chronic vertebrogenic pain; yet, its molecular mechanisms and clinical efficacy require critical appraisal. This narrative review highlights the milestones of osteoreception and elucidates the molecular mechanisms driving intraosseous receptor irritation and its pivotal role in chronic pain development. Pathological vertebral bone remodeling triggers a receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B ligand/osteoprotegerin (RANKL/OPG) imbalance, accelerating hyperactive osteoclastogenesis. Enhanced osteoclastic vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) expression drives microenvironment acidity and intraosseous hypertension, persistently stimulating acid-sensing ion channel 3 (ASIC3) and purinergic P2X2/3 receptors on intraosseous afferents. Concurrently, upregulated nerve growth factor (NGF) binds to tropomyosin receptor kinase A (TrkA), driving peripheral sensitization via transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) phosphorylation. The available clinical studies investigating intraosseous LTPI for vertebrogenic pain are scarce and heterogeneous, focusing primarily on low back pain, cervicalgia, and residual chronic pain after degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis decompression surgery. The reviewed data provide preliminary signals of potential benefit, observing a statistically significant analgesic effect of intraosseous LTPI within the studied cohorts. In two trials comparing it to intramuscular LTPI, one of which utilized a randomized controlled design, the intraosseous approach was reported to provide more pronounced short-term pain relief. However, these trials are limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous designs, and a lack of active long-term safety monitoring. Nevertheless, although current data provide promising but still limited insights, future double-blinded, multicenter randomized controlled trials are required to comprehensively establish the clinical efficacy, safety profile, and prolonged effect of intraosseous LTPI in the treatment of vertebrogenic pain.

Article.Title: Beyond Taxonomy: Fungal Nutraceutical Supplementation Modifies the Functional Potential of the Gut Microbiome in Colorectal Cancer
Article.Authors: Rodríguez-Costas N.; Rodríguez-Blanco A.; Expósito C.; Cubiella J.; Stompel E.; Fernández-de-Ana Portela C.; Martín A.; Taboada-Rodríguez P.; Silva B.; Fernández M.; Zarraquiños S.; Remedios D.; Gómez C.; Lorenzo S.; Poceiro R.; Parga M.; Ramírez V.; Pérez-Castro S.
Article.Abstract: The gut microbiome is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of host immune regulation, intestinal homeostasis, and recovery after colorectal cancer (CRC) surgery. Although our previous randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial demonstrated that fungal nutraceutical supplementation with Micodigest® was associated with favorable taxonomic and systemic inflammatory changes in patients undergoing CRC surgery with curative intent, the functional consequences of this intervention remain poorly understood. Here, we performed a functional metagenomic analysis of fecal samples collected from patients enrolled in the original clinical trial to investigate whether Micodigest® supplementation was associated with changes in the functional potential of the gut microbiome. A total of 37 patients were analyzed, including 24 receiving Micodigest® and 13 receiving placebo, with paired samples collected before supplementation and after 4–6 weeks of intervention. Shallow shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed, and microbial functional potential was characterized using KEGG Orthologues (KOs). Differential abundance analysis identified 14 significantly different KOs between groups at baseline and 23 after intervention, with no overlap between the two sets of orthologues. Following supplementation, Micodigest®-treated patients exhibited increased representation of functions related to CRISPR-associated systems, bacteriophage biology, and chitin-derived carbohydrate utilization, together with reduced representation of nutrient acquisition systems, conjugative transfer, sulfur metabolism, and components of the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway. These functional signatures suggest coordinated changes in microbial ecological adaptation, nutrient utilization, genetic exchange, and metabolic activity following fungal nutraceutical supplementation. Integration with previously reported taxonomic and inflammatory findings supports the hypothesis that Micodigest® may promote coordinated remodeling of the gut microbiome and host–microbiota interactions during the perioperative period. Although the present study cannot establish causality or directly infer microbial activity from metagenomic potential, these findings provide novel functional insights into the microbiome response to fungal nutraceutical supplementation in patients with CRC and highlight functional metagenomics as a valuable complement to taxonomic profiling.

Article.Title: Bone Morphogenetic Protein-2 and Cabozantinib for Temporomandibular Joint Cartilage Repair: Murine and Porcine Injury Models
Article.Authors: Silverstein M.; Hou S.; Ge C.; Garcia T.; Chan C.; Bruckman K.; Takematsu E.
Article.Abstract: Temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis (TMJ OA) is characterized by progressive degeneration of the fibrocartilaginous articular surface. We previously demonstrated that combined bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibition promotes endogenous hyaline cartilage regeneration in appendicular joints. Whether this regenerative strategy can be extended to the specialized fibrocartilage of the TMJ remains unknown. In this study, we evaluated the regenerative potential of BMP-2 combined with cabozantinib, an FDA-approved multikinase inhibitor with activity against VEGF receptors, using complementary murine and porcine TMJ cartilage injury models. In mice, needle-induced abrasion of the mandibular condyle resulted in loss of the fibrocartilaginous articular surface and extracellular matrix; treatment with BMP-2 and cabozantinib was associated with improved cartilage architecture and increased fibrocartilage thickness. To examine translational feasibility, we developed a surgically accessible porcine TMJ cartilage defect model and demonstrated the technical feasibility of local BMP-2 and cabozantinib delivery with formation of repair tissue within the defect. Collectively, these findings provide preliminary evidence supporting further investigation of combined BMP-2 and cabozantinib for TMJ cartilage repair.

Article.Title: Multi-Target Regulation of Diabetic Nephropathy by Alkaloids: Molecular Targets, Signaling Pathways and Therapeutic Potential
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Li Q.; Chen W.; Zhou L.; Li R.; Zhou N.; Luo S.; Zhang L.; Wu X.; Xie Y.; Guo P.
Article.Abstract: In the context of the global diabetes epidemic, diabetic nephropathy (DN)—a condition directly associated with diabetes—has become the primary cause of end-stage renal disease, significantly impacting patients’ quality of life and placing substantial demands on public healthcare resources. The pathogenesis of DN is characterized by metabolic disturbances induced by high glucose levels, hemodynamic abnormalities, and the synergistic amplification of various stress signals. These factors collectively contribute to the progressive loss of nephrons and irreversible renal dysfunction. Although current standard treatments can partially slow disease progression, they significantly fail to meet clinical needs. Therefore, there is an urgent necessity to identify multi-target intervention strategies that utilize novel mechanisms of action. Alkaloids, a class of natural nitrogen-containing compounds known for their significant structural diversity, have recently demonstrated multiple renoprotective effects in experimental models of DN. This review is based on a search of the PubMed, Web of Science and CNKI databases. The keywords alkaloids, diabetic nephropathy, diabetic nephropathies, diabetic kidney disease, inflammation, oxidative stress, fibrosis, autophagy and apoptosis were used to search for original research articles in both Chinese and English, published between 2010 and 2026, which investigated the mechanisms by which alkaloid compounds exert their anti-DN effects. Focusing on anti-inflammatory effects, anti-oxidative stress, anti-renal fibrosis, autophagy modulation, apoptosis regulation and ferroptosis inhibition, the review then summarized the relevant literature by systematizing the experimental models, intervention protocols, dosages and key results. This provided a new theoretical perspective and experimental basis for the clinical translation and new drug development of alkaloid compounds for the treatment of DN. The review provides a new theoretical perspective and an experimental basis for the clinical translation of, and new drug development based on, alkaloid compounds for the treatment of DN.

Article.Title: From Genes to Gonads: Molecular Control Points of Reproduction in the Sea Urchin as a Framework for Aquaculture
Article.Authors: Rodríguez A.; Olmos J.
Article.Abstract: The economic output of sea urchin aquaculture depends almost entirely on a single organ. Gonads, marketed as uni, determine value through their size, color, texture and flavor, and feed formulations have been optimized empirically for decades with limited reference to the molecular machinery governing gametogenesis, sex differentiation and gonadal maturation in echinoids. This review integrates four lines of mechanistic evidence around the adult gonad, namely developmental gene regulatory networks, sex-biased gonadal transcriptomics, germ-cell and nutritive-phagocyte biology, and endocrine, neuroendocrine and retinoid signaling, and reads them in terms of the control points connecting molecular state to production outcome. Rather than advancing a unified mechanistic model, which the current evidence does not support, each component is classified by the strength of the evidence attached to it: demonstrated in an echinoid, inferred from another taxon, plausible but untested, or hypothetical. The resulting picture is one in which descriptive resources have outpaced functional tests. Candidate sex-determination transcription factors have been identified but none have yet been directly perturbed in an echinoid, the retinoid pathway is architecturally present yet biochemically incomplete, and responses to exogenous steroids remain heterogeneous across species and protocols. Priority experimental directions are ranked by commercial return and by experimental falsifiability.

Article.Title: Molecular Mechanisms Underlying Progression and Spontaneous Regression in Desmoid Tumors
Article.Authors: Miwa S.; Hayashi K.; Higuchi T.; Yonezawa H.; Morinaga S.; Asano Y.; Demura S.
Article.Abstract: Desmoid-type fibromatosis, also known as desmoid tumor (DT), is a rare and locally aggressive soft tissue neoplasm driven by constitutive activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, most commonly through CTNNB1 or APC alterations. While some tumors progress and cause substantial morbidity, approximately 25–38% undergo spontaneous regression during active surveillance, which is currently recommended as the first-line management strategy. Although advances in next-generation sequencing and transcriptomic profiling have elucidated the molecular drivers of tumor progression, the molecular mechanisms underlying spontaneous regression remain poorly understood. This review summarizes current knowledge of the molecular pathogenesis of DT and proposed mechanisms of spontaneous regression, including attenuation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, hormonal modulation, alterations in the immune microenvironment, and crosstalk between Wnt signaling and other pathways such as Notch, PDGFR/c-Abl/HIF1α, and TGF-β. Based on the current knowledge of the molecular mechanisms in DT, spontaneous regression appears to reflect a multifactorial transition from an active proliferative state toward a quiescent, fibrotic phenotype rather than a single molecular event. Further studies integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics with immune profiling are warranted to identify therapeutic targets and stratify patients for active surveillance versus active treatment.

Article.Title: Low Nephron Number and Kidney Disease
Article.Authors: Goorani S.; Imig J.
Article.Abstract: Reduced nephron endowment and acquired nephron loss increase susceptibility to hypertension and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Low birth weight, prematurity, genetic factors, and adverse prenatal exposures can limit nephron development, whereas aging and kidney injury reduce the number of functioning nephrons after birth. Compensatory glomerular hypertrophy and increased single-nephron filtration can initially preserve overall glomerular filtration rate, but sustained glomerular stress may promote podocyte injury, proteinuria, and glomerulosclerosis. These changes can accelerate nephron loss and create a cycle of progressive kidney damage. Disease susceptibility depends on genetic background and additional metabolic, environmental, and hemodynamic stresses. This review examines the determinants of nephron number, the adaptive and potentially harmful consequences of nephron reduction, and approaches to preserving kidney function. Improving maternal health, reducing harmful exposures, and controlling hypertension and metabolic disease may reduce the long-term consequences of low nephron number.

Article.Title: Biopriming of Durum Wheat Seeds with Diazotrophic Bacteria Improved Physiological and Biochemical Pathways Under Salt Stress
Article.Authors: Hadj Brahim A.; Said Z.; Frikha E.; Jlidi M.; Ben Ali M.; Ben Ali M.
Article.Abstract: A significant strategy for sustainable management, by decreasing the use of chemical fertilizers, can consist of technology based on suitable levels of plant growth promoting bacteria (PGPB) seed biopriming. The main goal of this work was to demonstrate the positive effect of PGPB as seed biopriming factor on the growth of durum wheat plantlets under stress. plantlets physiological and biochemical pathways modifications were assessed in controlled growth chamber under salt stress. Seeds bioprimed with bacterial strains, in particular, Bacillus pumilus (MA9), Virgibacillus halodenitrificans (MA14), Bacillus subtilis (MA17), and Bacillus pumilus (MA19), demonstrated the best development of durum wheat seedlings under salt stress. The total length and total dry weight were altogether higher in bioprimed than in unbioprimed plants. The PGPB-bioprimed plants were very sound and hydrated, and the unbioprimed plant leaves were parched within 120 mM NaCl. In contrast to explants without PGPB, all the biochemical variables, for example, auxin, proline, soluble sugars, amino acids, and protein, were essentially improved in bioprimed explants. Biopriming with MA17 fundamentally diminished the reactive oxygen species (ROS) rate, particularly without salt stress. In any case, this impact of the hindrance of “ROS” was more pronounced under stressful conditions. The explant antioxidant prevention agent pathways catalase (CAT) and ascorbate peroxidase (APX) and the chlorophyll content were improved after seed biopriming with PGPB when explants with unbioprimed seeds had low cell reinforcement pathways under the two treatments, particularly under pressure. The bioprimed plants additionally had higher K+/Na+ proportions and expanded intracellular K+ ion activity. Hence, it can be anticipated that seed biopriming with PGPB is a novel technology that can improve healthy plant development under saline conditions. This study shows that PGPB has a significant effect in initiating resistance under stressful conditions in plants and can be utilized to develop new bioinoculants to reduce the use of chemical fertilizers.

Article.Title: A Proposed Convergent Genetic and Molecular Framework for Legg–Calvé–Perthes Disease: A Scoping Review
Article.Authors: Hernández-Zamora E.; Rodríguez-Olivas A.; Galicia-Alvarado M.; Casas-Ávila L.; Reyes-Maldonado E.
Article.Abstract: Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease (LCPD) is a rare pediatric disorder characterized by avascular osteonecrosis of the femoral head. Its pathogenesis is multifactorial, and genetic, epigenetic, vascular, and inflammatory mechanisms may contribute to disease susceptibility and progression. To map and characterize the available evidence on genetic and epigenetic factors and molecular pathways associated with LCPD, with particular emphasis on potential interactions and convergence across biological pathways. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR, PRISMA 2020 for Abstracts checklist). PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for studies published between March 2006 and March 2026. Relevant genetic, epigenetic, and molecular findings were extracted and synthesized according to biological pathways. See the PRISMA 2020 for Abstracts checklist. Seventeen genes and 25 single-nucleotide variants (SNVs), as reported in the included literature, were identified and grouped into three major biological axes: hypercoagulability, inflammation, and bone metabolism and remodeling. Associations with LCPD were reported in at least one study for F5 rs6025, MTHFR rs1801133, IL6 rs1800795, IL23R rs1569922, NOS3 rs1799983 and rs2070744, and OPG rs2073618. Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation and microRNA dysregulation, were also reported. Interpretation was limited by methodological heterogeneity, small study populations, limited functional validation, and a predominance of observational studies. Accumulating evidence suggests that thrombotic, inflammatory, bone remodeling, and epigenetic mechanisms contribute to LCPD susceptibility and pathogenesis. Our findings point to a potential biological convergence among these pathways; however, whether this convergence stems from a shared genetic architecture remains to be fully elucidated. LCPD pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of coagulation, inflammation, bone remodeling, and epigenetic pathways. While these mechanisms suggest biological convergence, their precise shared genetic architecture remains uncertain. Consequently, future studies utilizing independent replication and functional validation are critically needed.

Article.Title: Meta-Inflammation in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Theoretical, Methodological, and Clinical Aspects
Article.Authors: Zhuravleva Y.; Gusev E.
Article.Abstract: Currently, there is no doubt that insulin resistance (IR) in prediabetes and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with chronic systemic metabolic inflammation (SMI). SMI is typically considered a form of low-grade systemic inflammation (LGSI). At the same time, one cannot rule out the possibility of the transformation of LGSI into more pronounced forms of chronic systemic inflammation (ChSI), typical of systemic autoimmune diseases and characterized by a high severity of systemic inflammatory response (SIR). The aim of this research is to assess the pathogenetic role of SMI as a general pathological process in the pathogenesis of prediabetes and T2DM, as well as differentiating SMI into LGSI and ChSI. The study included two main groups—T2DM (n = 65) and prediabetes (n = 24)—as well as three control groups of healthy individuals of different ages (n = 50, n = 89, and n = 22). In the patients of the main groups, metabolic syndrome (MetS) was diagnosed in accordance with the American Heart Association criteria, and metabolic indices (HOMA-IR, HOMA-islet, and TyG) were calculated. The levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) and cytokines (TNFα, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-10) were determined in blood plasma as SIR parameters, and the levels of cortisol (690 nmol/L or <100 nmol/L), D-dimer (>250 and >500 ng/mL), and troponin I (>0.2 ng/mL) were used as additional SMI criteria. Based on molecular inflammatory markers, the ChSI and LGSI scales were calculated using the authors’ original method. SMI in T2DM and prediabetes manifested itself as both LGSI (in 57% of cases in T2DM and 46% in prediabetes) and ChSI (in 18.5% of cases in T2DM and 8.3% in prediabetes). The verification of SMI based on the frequently used criterion of CRP levels above 3 mg/L turned out to be ineffective in our study (this criterion was detected in the control groups in 24–45%). Therefore, we used CRP > 10 mg/L in combination with cytokines as the SIR criterion. Additionally, we identified the SMI criteria: D-dimer > 250 ng/mL in 27.7% of T2DM and 0% in the control groups and prediabetes; cortisol 15.4% in T2DM and 8.3% in prediabetes; and troponin I 7.7% in T2DM and 4.2% in prediabetes. SMI (LGSI and ChSI) develops in the majority of patients with prediabetes (54.1%) and T2DM (75.4%). To assess SMI, it is advisable to use the integral SIR criteria in combination with the markers of chronic stress, tissue damage, and coagulopathy.

Article.Title: Integrative Phosphoproteomic Characterization of ULK1 Phosphosites Reveals Co-Regulatory Networks in Autophagy and Metabolic Adaptation
Article.Authors: Basha F.; Kammarambath S.; Dcunha L.; Mahin A.; Gopalakrishnan A.; Sambreena A.; Madar I.; Raju R.
Article.Abstract: Unc-51-like autophagy-activating kinase 1 (ULK1), a serine/threonine kinase, is the central regulator of autophagy initiation and plays a crucial role in cellular homeostasis, metabolic adaptation, and stress responses. We performed a large-scale phosphoproteomic data analysis of ULK1 by systematically integrating and analyzing 891 profiling and 245 differential human phosphoproteomic datasets. S450, S623, and S638 emerged as the predominant phosphosites in ULK1, with the highest frequency of detection across multiple cellular phosphoproteomics datasets. Conservation analysis showed that these phosphosites are conserved across mammalian species and human ULK1 and ULK2 (Unc-51-like autophagy-activating kinase 2). The co-regulatory networks associated with these phosphosites, including interacting proteins, upstream kinases, and downstream substrates, were systematically analyzed. The phosphosite co-regulated ULK1 interactome revealed a network of associations linking ubiquitin-dependent cargo recognition to autophagosome biogenesis, trafficking, and maturation, indicating that ULK1 phosphoregulation may extend beyond its established role in autophagy initiation and be associated with multiple stages of selective autophagy. Notably, ULK1 phosphosites were linked to key metabolic enzymes in glycogen, sphingolipid, phospholipid, and glycolytic pathways, as well as classical lipolysis. Protein-normalized analysis across 12 cancer cohorts showed significant upregulation of the predominant ULK1 phosphosites, most frequently at S450 and S623. Comparative analysis with an independent ULK1/2 knockout phosphoproteomic dataset further supported the relevance of these identified co-regulated protein phosphosites. Collectively, this study provides a phosphosite-resolved view of ULK1 regulation and identifies candidate phosphosites and associated proteins for future functional and mechanistic studies.

Article.Title: microRNA and Regulatory Networks of Human Macrophage During Leishmania major In Vitro Infection
Article.Authors: Habouria S.; Bali A.; Diotallevi A.; Ben-Cheikh A.; Atri C.; De Santi M.; Maestrini S.; Galluzzi L.; Laouini D.; Guerfali F.
Article.Abstract: Leishmania (L.) major modulates host microRNA (miR) expression to promote intracellular survival, yet the roles of specific miRs during early infection of human macrophages remain poorly defined. We investigated the dynamic regulation of miR-21-5p and miR-146a-5p in THP-1-derived macrophages infected with L. major over an early post-infection time course (3–48 h), alongside miR-30a-3p and miR-101-3p. Both miR-21-5p and miR-146a-5p were significantly upregulated during the early stages of infection (3–24 h) before declining by 48 h. Using antisense LNA inhibitors, we achieved independent single and dual silencing of both miRs, allowing us to dissect their functional contribution to host gene expression. In silico network analysis identified 887 shared and specific target genes, including NFKB1, MYC, STAT3, HIF1A, TNF, CXCL8, IL18, and XBP1. Silencing of miR-21-5p and miR-146a-5p at early time points relieved inhibitory control over several of these targets, notably increasing NF-κB, MYC, IL18 and XBP1 expression, and reducing TNF and sXBP1, consistent with their role as negative regulators of innate immune signaling. These findings identify miR-21-5p and miR-146a-5p as early, dynamic regulators of the human macrophage transcriptional response to L. major infection and identify their target genes as candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets in cutaneous leishmaniasis.

Article.Title: Association of PTH1R Gene Polymorphisms with Three-Dimensional Mandibular Morphology Across Three Recruitment Cohorts
Article.Authors: Shin D.; Kimura R.; Kim Y.; Adel M.; Ueda S.; Takahashi M.; Hikita Y.; Yamaguchi T.
Article.Abstract: Parathyroid hormone 1 receptor (PTH1R) regulates chondrocyte differentiation and mandibular condylar cartilage development, but its contribution to adult mandibular morphology remains unclear. We investigated associations of two PTH1R single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), rs724448 and rs2242116, with three-dimensional mandibular morphology in 448 orthodontic patients recruited in Japan (199), Korea (79), and Egypt (170). Salivary DNA was genotyped, and computed tomography images were analyzed using geometric morphometrics and conventional measurements. Multivariate Procrustes analysis evaluated overall mandibular shape. Cohort-specific regressions examined natural-log-transformed centroid size (ln(centroid size)), principal component scores, and conventional measurements, adjusting for sex and age and additionally for imaging modality in Japan. Estimates were combined using inverse-variance fixed-effect meta-analysis. Neither variant showed a significant whole-shape association after correction for two SNP tests. Secondary analyses yielded negative estimates for ln(centroid size) and nominal associations with selected anteroposterior dimensions and cohort-specific principal component scores. None remained significant after either Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction across 408 tests. These findings provide no statistically robust evidence linking either variant to adult mandibular morphology. Nominal findings require independent replication.

Article.Title: Proteomic and Molecular Biological Analyses of Response Mechanism in Rice (Oryza sativa L. cv. Koshihikari) Under Drought Stress
Article.Authors: Shohag S.; Yamaguchi H.; Hitachi K.; Tsuchida K.; Komatsu S.
Article.Abstract: Drought stress severely limits rice growth, while roots play a key role in sensing water deficits and triggering adaptive responses. To investigate time-dependent molecular responses in rice (Oryza sativa L. cv. Koshihikari) under drought stress induced by polyethylene glycol (PEG), seedlings were exposed to 10 and 20% PEG for 4 and 8 days, followed by morphological, proteomic, immunoblot, polymerase chain reaction, and ATP content analyses. Primary root length and total root fresh weight were significantly decreased with 20% PEG for 8 days compared with untreated. Proteomic analysis revealed changes in the abundance of rice root proteins under 20% PEG treatment between 4 and 8 days, with differentially abundant proteins enriched in Gene Ontology categories related to nuclear components, protein phosphorylation, and ATP binding. Selected proteins related to protein protection, redox-associated processes, and cytoskeletal responses were examined using immunoblot and polymerase chain reaction analyses. Glutathione S-transferase decreased and heat shock protein 70 increased with PEG for 8 days. The expression of NADPH-dependent codeinone reductase was upregulated and heat shock protein 17.9 was downregulated by PEG for 8 days. ATP content per unit fresh weight decreased in roots after PEG treatment. These results suggest that prolonged PEG-induced osmotic stress inhibits rice root growth through alterations in cellular energy status, the abundance of proteins involved in protein protection and glutathione S-transferase-mediated detoxification, and the expression of genes associated with reactive carbonyl species metabolism.

Article.Title: CFTR Functional Rescue and Heterogeneous Clinical Outcomes Following Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor Therapy in People with Cystic Fibrosis Carrying the W1282R Variant
Article.Authors: Kondratyeva E.; Efremova A.; Melyanovskaya Y.; Zhekaite E.; Sapelnikova M.; Milovanov M.; Shchagina O.; Voronkova A.; Sherman V.; Krasovsky S.; Kutsev S.; Goldshtein D.
Article.Abstract: The clinical response to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) in people with cystic fibrosis carrying the rare cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) variant W1282R has not been well characterized. We retrospectively analyzed 12 people with cystic fibrosis treated with ETI for 3–36 months in addition to ongoing standard CF therapy.
