We investigated the topographical relationship between dermo-epidermal detachment and junction-associated Laminin-Receptor/Ribosomal Protein SA (Laminin-R/RPSA) immunoreactivity in 25 full-thickness skin specimens from documented fatal electrocution cases. Detachment on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was initially classified as present, absent, or equivocal, with discordant or equivocal assessments subsequently adjudicated by a supervising observer. After adjudication, detachment was present in 22 specimens (88%) and absent in three (12%). All 22 specimens with detachment lacked detectable junction-associated Laminin-R/RPSA immunoreactivity at the corresponding interface, whereas all three specimens without detachment retained the signal. All 25 preserved perilesional regions showed retained immunoreactivity. The paired absolute difference in the proportion showing loss of immunoreactivity between lesion and perilesional sites was 88.0 percentage points (95% CI, 55.5–97.5; exact McNemar p < 0.0001). These findings demonstrate a consistent spatial correspondence between dermo-epidermal separation and localized loss of detectable Laminin-R/RPSA immunoreactivity. Because the antibody targets RPSA rather than laminin-332, the results do not directly establish laminin-332 damage. Laminin-R/RPSA immunohistochemistry may complement conventional H&E examination, but controlled comparative studies are required to determine specificity and reproducibility.

Article.Title: Pathway-Level Synthesis Reveals Contrast-Dependent Rat Brain Transcriptomic Responses to Alcohol
Article.Authors: An H.; Yu J.; Shao C.; Meng D.; Yang G.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Public rat brain transcriptomic studies differ in sampled region and alcohol paradigm, which complicates assessment of reproducible molecular responses. We assembled 12 datasets, including four primary region-resolved datasets (64 samples) from the hippocampus, ventral tegmental area, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens. Each dataset was analyzed separately and projected onto predefined addiction-related, exercise-related, and stress-related pathway axes; only aligned contrast-level effects were synthesized across datasets. In the closest available two-dataset comparison, both studies used adult male Sprague–Dawley rats, chronic liquid-diet exposure, and 24 h withdrawal. Withdrawal versus control showed directional agreement for all three original axes and their three deterministic derived indices, whereas chronic ethanol versus control agreed for only one of these six summaries. The derived indices do not constitute independent replication, and this two-study result is interpreted as contrast-specific directional concordance under similar protocols without identifying brain region as its cause. Across the broader alcohol-domain resource, effects occupied both directions and showed substantial between-contrast dispersion, defining a boundary to generalization rather than a universal alcohol response. The central interpretation was materially unchanged by alternative scoring algorithms, pathway catalogs, or cluster-balanced reanalysis of overlapping pathways; at a pathway-overlap (Jaccard similarity) threshold of 0.5, the latter preserved sample-level rankings (median Spearman ρ=0.983) and 76 of 78 pairwise effect directions. These results provide a reproducible framework for distinguishing local convergence from broader context dependence in rat alcohol transcriptomics. Candidate biomarkers should therefore be evaluated in harmonized exposure, withdrawal, region, sex, and species settings before translational interpretation.

Article.Title: Annexin A6 in Eye-Lavage Extracellular Vesicles—a Candidate Biomarker for Sex-Specific Differences in Mild Hypoxic–Ischaemic Brain Damage—Findings from an Explorative Neonatal Mouse Model Study
Article.Authors: Lange S.; Needham S.; Kraev I.; Davis B.; Hristova M.
Article.Abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) play important roles in cell communication, including via transfer of cargo proteins, and are promising biomarkers for pathobiological processes. Reliable biomarkers for mild neonatal hypoxia ischaemia (HI) are scarce. Wrongly determined HI severity often leads to adverse long-term neurological outcomes, with more detrimental effects in males. Therefore, identification of sex-specific markers for HI is of great interest. We recently reported the potential of EVs from eye lavage as novel non-invasive biomarkers of neonatal HI brain injury, differing in proteomic cargoes between mild and severe HI brain insults. In continuation, the current study therefore focused on assessing sex-specific differences in the same mouse model of mild HI with respect to Annexin A6 (ANXA6) EV protein cargo, at different time points (0 h, 24 h and 48 h) post HI insult. Using direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) quantifying and co-localising ANXA6 to EV subtypes, our results indicate more marked changes in males compared with females, with a peak of positive ANXA6 detection in EVs at 24 h post HI in males. PanEV+TT+ EVs contained most ANXA6, followed by the PanEV+-labelled EVs. In the females, less ANXA6-positive staining was observed in EVs of all three time points in the HI groups compared with the males. In the sham and naïve control animals, ANXA6 detection suggested developmental reduction of ANXA6 in both sexes. However, in the male HI groups that developmental reduction was eliminated and ANXA6 remained at an increased level at all three time points. In addition, EV subtype labelling showed some differences between time points within each sex group and between sexes. PanEV+ single labelled EVs were more abundant in the females compared with the males in the 0 h and 24 h post-HI groups and PanEV+TT+-labelled EVs were more abundant in females than males at the 0 h post-HI time point. Our pilot findings indicate that increased ANXA6 labelling in eye-lavage EVs is associated with the mild HI model with more marked changes in males, where ANXA6 positivity peaked at 24 h post HI. Outcomes of this study contribute to EV-based biomarker development for HI diagnostics, with potential clinical value, including sex-specific differences. Future studies should include validation in further biological replicates in larger cohort sizes and assessment in human neonatal clinical samples.

Article.Title: Poly-L-Lactic Acid Attenuates Fibrotic Remodeling During Cutaneous Wound Healing
Article.Authors: Byun K.; Kim H.; Oh S.; Yu K.; Lee J.; Son K.; Byun K.
Article.Abstract: Pathological hypoxia following cutaneous injury is a critical driver of wound chronicity and fibrotic remodeling. The nuclear receptor binding SET domain protein 2 (NSD2)/lysine demethylase 2A (KDM2A)–histone H3 lysine 36 dimethylation (H3K36me2) axis is a known regulator of hypoxia-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in malignancy; however, its role in skin repair remains largely unexplored. We investigated whether poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) could attenuate fibrotic remodeling by modulating the NSD2/KDM2A–H3K36me2 axis and examining angiogenic signaling. We used a murine 9 mm punch-wound model for in vivo assessment and HaCaT keratinocytes and human dermal fibroblasts (HDFs) exposed to 2% O2 as in vitro hypoxia models. PLLA was administered to evaluate its impact on angiogenic signaling, collagen architecture, and the NSD2/KDM2A pathway. PLLA was associated with increased angiogenic markers and reduced expression of several hypoxia-associated epigenetic and fibrotic markers. In mice, PLLA increased vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)/VEGF receptor 2 expression and blood vessel abundance. In addition, PLLA decreased NSD2 and H3K36me2 levels while increasing KDM2A levels. Histological analysis showed less dense collagen staining and a change in the collagen type I/type III staining ratio, alongside a smaller photographically defined residual lesion area. Under controlled hypoxic conditions in vitro, PLLA suppressed EMT-related transcription factors, including Snail, Slug, and Twist, in keratinocytes and attenuated transforming growth factor-β1/phosphorylated mothers against decapentaplegic homolog 2/3 signaling and α-smooth muscle actin expression in fibroblasts. These findings support further study of PLLA-associated changes in vascular, epithelial, and fibrotic markers during wound remodeling.

Article.Title: LOH, LST, and TAI Profiles in Solid Tumors Harboring Pathogenic or Likely Pathogenic BRCA1/2 Variants: An Exploratory Study
Article.Authors: Erdogdu S.; Ekinci B.; Orenay-Boyacioglu S.; Boyacioglu O.; Erdogdu I.; Meteoglu I.
Article.Abstract: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is a critical indicator of genomic instability; however, the composite HRD score may not reflect the distribution of distinct genomic scar components underlying this phenotype. In this exploratory study, we compared the absolute and relative contributions of loss of heterozygosity (LOH), large-scale state transitions (LST), and telomeric allelic imbalance (TAI) among solid tumors harboring pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants in BRCA1 or BRCA2. This retrospective study included 76 patients with solid tumors who underwent HRD testing between January 2023 and January 2026. P/LP variants in homologous recombination repair (HRR) genes, alongside LOH, LST, and TAI scores, were evaluated. The composite HRD score was calculated as LOH + LST + TAI, with values ≥ 56 defined as HRD-positive. Additionally, the relative contribution of each scar component to the total HRD score was determined. Given the small sizes of the BRCA1-only and BRCA2-only subgroups and the heterogeneity of the overall cohort, all gene-group comparisons were considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Overall, 21.1% of the cohort was HRD-positive. Patients harboring BRCA1/2 P/LP variants displayed a significantly higher median HRD score compared to non-carriers (47.0 vs. 30.0; p = 0.016). When comparing patients with tumors harboring BRCA1-only (n = 9) and BRCA2-only (n = 10) P/LP variants, LOH was higher in the BRCA2 group (19.0 vs. 5.0; p = 0.036); however, this difference did not retain statistical significance following false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment (q = 0.108). In an exploratory sensitivity analysis restricted to breast and ovarian tumors (BRCA1-only, n = 5; BRCA2-only, n = 9), the LOH/HRD ratio was higher in the BRCA2 group (0.301 vs. 0.000; p = 0.026; q = 0.039), whereas the LST/HRD ratio was higher in the BRCA1 group (0.488 vs. 0.310; p = 0.019; q = 0.039). These estimates were based on very small subgroups and should therefore be interpreted cautiously. This exploratory analysis identified differences in the relative distributions of LOH and LST between tumors harboring BRCA1-only and BRCA2-only P/LP variants, particularly in the breast/ovarian subset. However, the small and heterogeneous subgroups, together with the absence of systematic assessment of biallelic BRCA1/2 inactivation, preclude gene-specific or mechanistic conclusions. These observations should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger, tumor-specific, independent cohorts.

Article.Title: Parameter-Based Prioritization of Time-Resolved LC–HRMS Ion Tracks for Untargeted Reaction Monitoring
Article.Authors: Ilyasov I.; Braun A.; Olicheva V.; Goman V.; Grikh V.; Zhevlakova A.; Selivanova I.; Beloborodov V.
Article.Abstract: Herein, an automated, parameter-based workflow is introduced for processing time-resolved high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) data. Its utility is demonstrated using the reaction between the ABTS•+ radical cation and the polyphenolic antioxidant naringenin. Data were collected using HRMS coupled to high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) in negative ion mode. The algorithm compares sequential time-resolved HRMS measurements to generate kinetic curves and calculate parameters for every detected species. Based on these curves and parameters, we can tentatively classify each species as a reagent, intermediate, or product. The algorithm was implemented as Java-based software. As a result, extensive data arrays of 1.3 million m/z-intensity pairs per experimental series were processed automatically. The workflow generated manageable candidate sets in each replicate series. Cross-replicate matching using a 5 ppm mass tolerance retained 29 ion tracks consistently detected in all three reaction runs for subsequent analysis. These ions can then be examined manually to identify compound structures. Overall, the approach provides a screening tool for untargeted reaction monitoring and supports subsequent structural annotation in complex chemical systems.

Article.Title: Physiological and Molecular Mechanisms of Tree Responses to Combined Drought and Low-Nitrogen Stress: A Review
Article.Authors: Xu Y.; Yang Z.; Yu L.; Wang X.; Li C.; Wei M.
Article.Abstract: Drought and low nitrogen often co-occur in forests, yet their combined effects cannot be inferred reliably from single-stress studies. This review synthesizes physiological and molecular evidence for tree responses to combined drought and low nitrogen at four levels, namely stress perception, signal transduction, metabolic reprogramming, and adaptive phenotypes. It compares single-stress baselines and evaluates reported interactions in photosynthesis, water-use efficiency, root traits, and carbon–nitrogen allocation. The review distinguishes direct tree evidence from mechanistic context derived from crops and model plants. Abscisic acid–nitrogen signaling crosstalk is considered alongside reactive oxygen species, energy, hydraulics, and transcriptional regulation as candidate integration routes. Candidate genes are classified by species context and experimental evidence; responsiveness to the two single stresses is not interpreted as proof of a combined-stress function. The review also assesses the opportunities and current limitations of multi-omics and genome editing for trees. It identifies priorities for factorial experiments, multi-year validation, and molecular breeding for climate-resilient forestry.

Article.Title: Dynamic Immune Responsiveness in Breast Cancer: Tumor Microenvironment Plasticity, Therapeutic Timing, and Clinical Translation
Article.Authors: Udden S.; Obaid M.; Pop L.; Hannan R.
Article.Abstract: Breast cancer immunotherapy has advanced substantially, yet durable clinical benefit remains limited to selected patient populations, reflecting heterogeneity in tumor–immune interactions across molecular subtypes, disease stages, and treatment contexts. This review frames immune responsiveness as a dynamic manifestation of tumor microenvironmental plasticity rather than a fixed tumor phenotype. We integrate mechanistic evidence showing that anti-tumor immunity is governed by interactions among malignant cells, immune populations, and cancer-associated fibroblasts. We emphasize therapeutic timing where treatment-induced changes in antigen availability, immune priming, stromal architecture, and cellular composition may create transient windows of immune susceptibility. Mechanisms of immune escape, including defective antigen presentation, T-cell dysfunction, suppressive myeloid populations, stromal exclusion, vascular abnormalities, and metabolic constraints, are evaluated as potential therapeutic targets. Emerging approaches incorporating single-cell and spatial profiling, circulating tumor DNA, multiomics, digital pathology, and artificial intelligence offer approaches for longitudinal characterization of evolving immune states, but their clinical utility in guiding immunotherapy remains largely unvalidated. We propose a precision-immunotherapy framework in which treatment selection and sequencing could be informed by these states. This framework complements established treatment approaches and defines testable hypotheses for prospective clinical studies.

Article.Title: Mechanisms of Hypomagnetic Field Biological Effects: Quantum Rotator Versus Radical Pair
Article.Authors: Binhi V.; Usovik I.; Koshel I.
Article.Abstract: The radical pair mechanism (RPM) struggles to explain the biological effects of weak magnetic fields due to rapid spin decoherence. To address this, we propose a mechanism based on the quantum dynamics of a sub-nanometric (<0.5 nm) molecular rotator modeling an amino acid residue within a biosynthesizing enzyme. Using the Liouville–von Neumann equation with chemical kinetics and phenomenological decoherence, we show that MF effects arise from modulation of the rotator’s quantum interference pattern rather than from spin prohibition. Our results demonstrate that effects reaching several tens of percent occur in very weak magnetic fields (below 50 μT), are relatively robust to decoherence, and that while temperature promotes decoherence, it also enables the formation of a magnetic field-sensitive interference pattern. Under realistic parameters, the angular distribution of the rotator’s probability density rotates by several degrees in the geomagnetic field. The rotator mechanism implies that evolution has adapted organisms to use the geomagnetic field for nearly error-free biosynthesis; under hypomagnetic fields, biosynthetic errors increase. Unlike the RPM, this mechanism achieves high sensitivity by operating via magnetic field-induced phase changes rather than magnetic moment energy, thereby circumventing the standard quantum limit. Although tentative and lacking direct experimental evidence, the quantum rotator mechanism provides a biophysically transparent interpretation of hypomagnetic field effects, magnetic storms, and animal magnetic navigation, opening new avenues for research and various applications.

Article.Title: Placental Iron Homeostasis: Navigating the Delicate Balance Between Transport and Ferroptosis
Article.Authors: Szukiewicz D.
Article.Abstract: As an essential micronutrient, iron plays a vital role in oxygen transport, deoxyribonucleic acid synthesis, and energy production and is a redox-active cofactor for many biological processes. However, ferrous iron (Fe2+) is toxic to cells because it reacts with hydrogen peroxide in the Fenton reaction to generate the hydroxyl (free) radical, a key player in oxidative stress, leading to lipid peroxidation and iron-dependent cell death (ferroptosis). Therefore, iron homeostasis is precisely regulated. Maintaining appropriate iron metabolism during pregnancy is a major challenge, as it requires adaptation at the level of the utero–placental–fetal unit to the dynamic changes in the demand for iron in the developing fetus during the later weeks of pregnancy. The distinction between physiological (normal) anemia, which results from hemodilution and leads to the depletion of intracellular iron stores (ferritin) in placental cells, and the manifestation of the toxic effects of iron overload and/or oxidative stress is not always clear. Moreover, chronic inflammation during pregnancy associated with increasingly common metabolic disorders such as obesity, diabetes and hypertension may induce ferroptosis. This review presents the current understanding of placental iron homeostasis and its disturbances, focusing on the role of ferroptosis in placental dysfunction. The rationale for potentially effective anti-ferroptotic treatment is also presented.

Article.Title: Heterologous Expression and Immunoreactivity of Wheat Amylase–Trypsin Inhibitors
Article.Authors: Call L.; Svoboda T.; Krisai A.; Hacker T.; Lauter K.; D’Amico S.; Linhart B.; Amouric A.; Lafond M.; Giardina T.; Ebisawa M.; Valenta R.; Grausgruber H.
Article.Abstract: Wheat amylase–trypsin inhibitors (ATIs) are known for their allergenic properties, but their precise role in celiac disease and other wheat-related disorders remains unclear. Pure ATI preparations provide a basis for detailed biochemical and immunologic characterization; however, the complexity of isolating ATIs in the absence of other immunoreactive wheat proteins is an ongoing challenge. To address this limitation, bacterial and yeast heterologous expression systems were evaluated for the production of pure ATI preparations. While the synthesis of recombinant ATIs 0.28 and CM3 in Escherichia coli was challenging regarding protein solubility, promising results were observed for ATIs 0.19, CM1 and CM3 expressed in Pichia pastoris, both in terms of solubility and protein yields. The biochemical and immunoreactive properties of these recombinant ATIs were evaluated by SDS-PAGE, MALDI-TOF MS, LC-MS/MS, circular dichroism analysis, and in vitro inhibitory and immunoassays, and compared to native ATIs isolated from wheat. Our findings shed light on the difficulties in isolating pure ATIs and provide valuable insights into the potential impact of these proteins on human health. By using innovative expression systems, we aim to contribute to the detailed biochemical and immunogenic characterization of ATIs and improve the understanding of their role in wheat-related disorders and associated allergic responses.

Article.Title: Nanoscale Analysis of SSB–RecO Interplay in SSB Interaction with the Target
Article.Authors: Irukuvajjula S.; Filliaux S.; Lyubchenko Y.
Article.Abstract: Single-stranded DNA-binding protein (SSB) coats single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and recruits downstream factors, yet this same coating must be cleared for SSB-interacting proteins to bind. RecA is a central protein in homologous recombination, which requires SSB-free ssDNA to load during the process. RecO, a recombination mediator protein, is thought to regulate this handoff, but it has not been shown directly that RecO drives the release of full-length, ssDNA-bound SSB. Using atomic force microscopy, we show that RecO actively displaces full-length wild-type SSB from a defined ssDNA substrate, reducing occupancy from 67% to 29%. Displacement efficiency decreases after deleting the C-terminal tip of SSB (ΔC8) or after adding a single alanine at the C-terminus of SSB (A179). Molecular dynamics simulations show that A179 retains its native RecO contact but additionally engages a non-native surface, producing a specific, over-engaged complex, suggesting that these interprotein interactions may affect SSB-ssDNA contacts. Together, these findings suggest that RecO-driven SSB clearance is governed by the protein–protein interface rather than by ssDNA-binding affinity alone, thereby acting as a checkpoint against indiscriminate SSB removal during genome maintenance.

Article.Title: Bench-to-Bedside Perspectives on the Development of Soluble TCR-Based Protein Biologics: Current Landscape, Control Strategy and Future Direction
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; An H.; Yu C.; Li W.; Li M.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: Soluble T-cell receptor (TCR)-based biologics (protein-based) are an emerging class of immunotherapeutic agents that recognize antigenic peptides presented by the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) on the surface of target cells. Furthermore, they simultaneously bind to cluster of differentiation 3 (CD3) subunits on T cells, recruit T cells to target cells, and promote T-cell activation and degranulation, ultimately eliminating tumor cells. Soluble TCR-based protein biologics target intracellular antigens that are inaccessible to conventional antibody-based drugs. Consequently, the development of soluble TCR-based protein biologics has generated significant interest. One soluble TCR-based protein biologic is already approved for marketing, and several other drugs are entering clinical stages. Soluble TCR-based protein biologics have substantial therapeutic benefits but may cause cytokine release syndrome (CRS), off-target toxicity, and drug resistance. This review outlines the structural characteristics and mechanisms of action of soluble TCR-based protein biologics, introduces nonclinical research concerning soluble TCR-based protein biologics, describes the clinical progress, discusses the quality control of TCR drugs, and explores the challenges and possible future improvements for soluble TCR-based protein biologics.

Article.Title: Bioprospecting of Cheese Whey: Isolation, Safety and Cytoprotective Effects of Limosilactobacillus fermentum Strains on Intestinal Cells
Article.Authors: Díaz Vergara L.; Bettiol M.; Centomo A.; Cavaglieri L.; Montenegro M.; Rossi Y.
Article.Abstract: Bioprospecting is the identification and exploitation of natural resources for commercial purposes. Cheese whey is a major dairy by-product rich in nutrients and a possible source of bioactive compounds. The aim of this study was to isolate and identify lactic acid bacteria from cheese whey and characterize them based on their probiotic and technological properties, together with their cytotoxicity and cytoprotective effect on intestinal epithelial cells. From 142 isolates, three were selected as potential probiotic strains; all three were identified as Limosilactobacillus fermentum by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The strains co-aggregated with pathogenic bacteria (up to 52.7%), scavenged the ABTS●+ radical cation (10–70%), produced 374–459 mg/L of exopolysaccharides and tolerated sucrose, NaCl and CaCl2 at the concentrations tested. L. fermentum VM016, VM023 and VM030 showed no cytotoxicity at 107 CFU/mL and showed a cytoprotective effect against the oxidative stress of menadione at concentrations as low as 104 CFU/mL in IEC-18 cells, and 105 CFU/mL in Caco-2 cells. These results show that cheese whey retains a cultivable lactic acid bacteria fraction already adapted to the physicochemical conditions of the dairy matrix, from which autochthonous cultures can be recovered exhibiting probiotic potential, technological suitability, and favorable preliminary safety indicators for human consumption.

Article.Title: Highlights in Cysteine Protease Inhibitors as Antiparasitic Agents Against Trypanosomatids
Article.Authors: Querido B.; Sousa M.; Salvador J.
Article.Abstract: Trypanosoma cruzi, Trypanosoma brucei and Leishmania spp. are the causative agents of Chagas disease, human African trypanosomiasis, and leishmaniasis, respectively. These three neglected tropical diseases affect millions of individuals globally, and current therapeutic options remain severely limited. The major cysteine proteases (CPs) of these parasites play critical roles in their infectivity and survival, making them subjects of prolonged research. Therefore, cruzain, TbrCATL and CPB from Leishmania spp. have been recognized as the primary targets of most drugs under investigation. Among the diverse chemical classes investigated as cathepsin L-like inhibitors, natural compounds derivatives (including compounds derived from curcumin, Gallinamide A, and flavonoids) as well as molecules containing Michael acceptors, and nitrile and thiosemicarbazone moieties, have emerged as particularly promising scaffolds. The aim of this review is to provide an overview of the advances made over the last decade in the discovery and optimization of CP inhibitors with antitrypanosomal and antileishmanial activity, emphasizing their chemical scaffolds, biological activities, and therapeutic potential.

Article.Title: Associations of Serum Cartilage Oligomeric Matrix Protein with Body Composition and Hematological Inflammatory Indices in Postmenopausal Women
Article.Authors: Wojciechowski M.; Nowak A.; Ogurkowska M.; Podgórski T.; Leszczyński P.; Huta-Osiecka A.; Wochna K.
Article.Abstract: In the postmenopausal period, a decrease in sex hormone levels may alter body composition and can predispose individuals to increased body fat and musculoskeletal tissue degeneration, including a deterioration in the articular cartilage. The aim of the study was to assess the resting serum cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) concentrations in postmenopausal women with different body mass indexes (BMIs) and how COMP correlates with both lean and fat mass as well as with blood count-derived inflammatory markers. Thirty-three postmenopausal women were included in the study. Total fat and lean body mass were measured via dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry. Blood serum concentrations of COMP and adiponectin were assessed, and lymphocyte, monocyte and granulocyte counts were determined. The lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR) and granulocyte-to-lymphocyte (GLR) ratios were calculated. The analysis of differences in body mass, BMI, lean body mass, fat mass, and android (p ≤ 0.01) and gynoid fat mass (p < 0.05) revealed significantly lower values in the group of women with a normal BMI compared to the group with a BMI above the normal range. In the group of women with a normal BMI, a significant relationship was noted between COMP and lean body mass (p ≤ 0.01). In the group of women with a BMI above the normal range, a significant positive correlation of COMP with LMR (p < 0.05) and a negative correlation with GLR (p < 0.05) were observed. The significant associations between resting serum COMP levels and lean body mass and inflammatory markers, which varied according to BMI categories, suggest that body composition may be an important factor to consider when using COMP for diagnostic purposes.

Article.Title: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Data in Metastatic Melanoma with Pre-Existing Autoimmune Disease: A Real World Experience
Article.Authors: Vitale M.; Mallardo D.; Sparano F.; Festino L.; Vanella V.; Trojaniello C.; Ottaviano M.; Cioli E.; Mallardo M.; Facchini B.; Simeone E.; Ascierto P.
Article.Abstract: Patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease (AID) are underrepresented in trials of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). We retrospectively compared 41 patients with stage IV melanoma and pre-existing AID with 162 contemporaneous controls without AID who received ICI treatment between November 2016 and April 2023. In the AID and control cohorts, respectively, the objective response rates were 46.3% and 32.7%, and the disease control rates were 80.5% and 51.2%. Treatment interruption attributed to worsening of the baseline AID was recorded in 11/41 patients, while 13/41 interrupted treatment because of toxicity distinct from the baseline AID. The full cohort contributed 114 progression-free survival (PFS) events and 92 deaths. In models adjusted for age, sex, ICI regimen and M category, AID was associated with PFS (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.48, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.24–0.99; p = 0.046), whereas the association with overall survival (OS) was not statistically significant (adjusted HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.29–1.34; p = 0.232). These findings support the feasibility of ICI therapy in carefully selected patients with clinically stable AID, while the observational design and residual confounding require cautious interpretation of comparative outcomes.

Article.Title: Comparison of SERS Substrates in Direct Analysis of Urine Samples for Detection of Albuminuria: Relatively Large Gold Nano-Spheroids Outperform Gold Nanorods on Gold Film
Article.Authors: Boranova A.; Kabyl A.; Tuleuov B.; Kassymaly M.; Makhammajanov Z.; Gaipov A.; Bukasov R.
Article.Abstract: Proteins found in human urine can be used as a source of information on kidney function and as possible biomarkers for diseases such as chronic kidney disease (CKD). Focusing on differentiating between high and low albumin concentrations in urine samples, this study examines the roles of various substrates in detecting albuminuria as a specific form of proteinuria using surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS). Using gold nanorods (AuNRs) and gold spheroidal nanoparticles (AuNPs) on various substrates to optimize the identification of albuminuria, we studied urine samples from 77 and 124 patients with albumin concentrations above and below 0.3 g/L. SERS spectra were analyzed using principal component analysis—linear discriminant analysis (PCA-LDA), partial least squares with linear discriminant analysis (PLS-LDA), and support vector machine (PLS-SVM)—to differentiate between high- and low-urinary-albumin groups. PLS-LDA was the best-performing method among the three methods. The largest of all tested nanoparticles, 200 nm diameter (D200 nm) AuNPs on gold substrates, performed best in distinguishing between high and low concentrations of albumin in urine, with a maximum average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.97, 100% sensitivity, 92% specificity, and 96% accuracy and a higher enhancement factor of 5.4 × 107 in comparison to the same parameters obtained with λ650 nm and λ750 nm AuNRs on gold, which demonstrated average AUC values of 0.86 and 0.77 and EFs of 11 and 3 × 106, respectively. These larger NPs create hot spots in nanogaps between nanoparticles, which may have better accessibility to protein molecules compared to hot spots created in gaps between smaller nanorods and nanoparticles. This study highlights the role of nanoparticle size and shape in determining optimal SERS substrate parameters, thereby yielding more accurate results in the detection of high concentrations of albumin in urine by direct SERS.

Article.Title: Celastrol in Rheumatoid Arthritis: Immunomodulatory Mechanisms, Multicellular Convergence, and Translational Challenges
Article.Authors: Corona-Meraz F.; Martín-Márquez B.; Cobos-Puc L.; Guzmán-Alemán E.; Aguayo-Morales H.; Hernández-Ortega L.; Rosales-Gómez R.; Castañeda-Arellano R.; Sandoval-García F.; Tovar-Cuevas A.
Article.Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) arises from interactions among immune, stromal, and osteoimmune compartments, supporting interest in agents with multilevel activity, such as celastrol. This narrative review critically integrates evidence on its chemical–pharmacological basis, immunomodulatory mechanisms, cellular effects, and translational potential in RA. Preclinical data show inhibition of inflammatory programs in macrophages and neutrophils, modulation of T- and B-cell responses, suppression of pathogenic fibroblast-like synoviocyte (FLS) functions, and reduced osteoclastogenesis and structural damage. COMM domain-containing proteins 3 and 8 (COMMD3/8) provide the strongest causal validation, while insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 3 (IGF2BP3) has biophysical and functional support; numerous inflammatory and metabolic nodes primarily represent downstream signaling. Multicellular models support functional convergence, but intercellular causation in RA remains limited; directional functional evidence for dendritic cell–T-cell modulation comes from non-rheumatoid models, and no persistent synovial reprogramming has been demonstrated. Low bioavailability, multitarget covalent pharmacology, a narrow therapeutic window, and contributions from delivery carriers constrain translational interpretation. Addressing these translational challenges explicitly can help guide future research to improve celastrol's safety and efficacy, which is essential for clinical application.

Article.Title: Water Inside the Carbon Cage—H2O@C60 and Related Fullerene Structures: Synthesis, Experimental Characterization, Computational Insights, and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zielińska-Pisklak M.; Kuś Z.; Gackowski M.; Szeleszczuk Ł.
Article.Abstract: The encapsulation of a single water molecule inside C60 has established H2O@C60 as a benchmark system for investigating molecular behavior under precisely defined subnanometer confinement. This review integrates advances in the synthesis, experimental characterization, theoretical description, and emerging applications of H2O@C60 and selected related water-containing fullerenes. Particular attention is given to molecular-surgery strategies, in which the fullerene cage is opened, loaded with water, and subsequently reconstructed, as well as to improvements that have increased encapsulation and cage-closure efficiencies and enabled isotopically labeled and heterofullerene derivatives. Structural, nuclear magnetic resonance, infrared, terahertz, neutron-scattering, dielectric, photoelectron, and single-molecule transport studies collectively show that the C60 framework remains highly rigid, while the confined water molecule retains pronounced translational, rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin dynamics. At the same time, weak but measurable host–guest interactions produce symmetry breaking, rotational-level splitting, electrostatic screening, modified vibrational responses, and environment-dependent ortho–para conversion. Computational studies, ranging from density functional and correlated wave-function methods to multidimensional quantum-dynamical and molecular-dynamics approaches, have been essential for interpreting these observations and defining the underlying potential-energy landscape. Related systems, including H2O@C70, H2O@C59N, charged azafullerenes, and isotopically substituted endofullerenes, provide routes to tune cage geometry and electrostatic interactions. Although technological applications remain largely at the proof-of-principle stage, these systems offer promising platforms for quantum spectroscopy, molecular electronics, and the rational design of functional host–guest nanomaterials.

Article.Title: Targeting the Microbiota–Metabolism–Immunity Axis: Active Components of Traditional Chinese Medicine in Colitis-Associated Colorectal Cancer
Article.Authors: Chen Q.; Zhang H.; Fu L.; Liu F.; Yang Q.; Zhang G.; Huang Y.; Yang Y.; Yao C.; Wang Y.; Du Z.; Luo H.
Article.Abstract: Colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC) develops in the setting of long-standing intestinal inflammation and remains a major complication of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Although effective control of inflammation may reduce cancer risk, approaches that specifically prevent the progression from chronic colitis to neoplasia remain limited. Disruption of the gut microbiota–metabolism–immunity axis is increasingly implicated in this process, as microbial dysbiosis and altered metabolite production can compromise epithelial barrier integrity, sustain inflammatory signaling, and disturb mucosal immune homeostasis. This review examines how active components derived from traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), particularly flavonoids, alkaloids, saponins, and polysaccharides, influence this interconnected network in CAC-related models. Rather than treating these constituents as a single group, we compare the mechanistic patterns and evidence base associated with each class. Flavonoids and alkaloids have been studied mainly in relation to inflammatory signaling and epithelial barrier protection, whereas saponins are more often linked to regulation of the immune microenvironment. Polysaccharides have been studied most frequently in relation to microbiota remodeling, short-chain fatty acid production, and mucosal immune balance. These distinctions are not absolute, and substantial overlap exists across component classes. Moreover, most evidence is derived from animal or cell-based studies, with marked variation in experimental models, compound characterizations, dosing, and outcome assessments. The microbiota–metabolism–immunity axis provides a coherent framework for interpreting the multi-level actions of TCM-derived components, but their causal mechanisms and clinical relevance to human CAC require further validation.

Article.Title: ISG15 Is a Key Multidirectional Regulator of Cytosolic RNA- and DNA-Sensing Pathways and Type I Interferon Feedback Loops
Article.Authors: White M.; Iordanskiy S.
Article.Abstract: Activation of cytosolic RNA and DNA sensing pathways that normally recognize viral nucleic acids triggers the expression and release of type I interferons (IFN-I). This release drives the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) that activate acute inflammation and counteract viral replication at various stages. Recent studies have highlighted how interferon-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15), a small, ubiquitin-like modifier, regulates cytosolic RNA and DNA sensing pathway proteins to control the antiviral response and inflammation. ISG15 is a multifunctional protein that acts as a secreted cytokine, binds freely to intracellular proteins, and covalently modifies proteins in a reversible process termed ISGylation. A dual regulatory molecule, ISG15 can both stabilize and destabilize proteins that promote and inhibit IFN-I signaling. Conversely, viruses have evolved strategies to disrupt and exploit ISG15-dependent antiviral responses to evade the host immune system. In this review, we examine how ISG15 regulates cytosolic RNA and DNA sensing pathway proteins to control IFN-I signaling and the antiviral response, highlighting it as a master regulator that fine-tunes IFN-I signaling and feedback. Recognizing the multifaceted action of ISG15 is essential for designing balanced therapeutic strategies across antiviral drug development, cancer immunotherapy, and chronic inflammatory disease management.

Article.Title: Biopsy-Based Molecular Signatures Predicting Therapeutic Response in Ulcerative Colitis
Article.Authors: Grassi I.; Liso M.; Mastronardi M.; Valentini A.; Curlo M.; Armentano R.; Cavalcanti E.
Article.Abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with marked molecular heterogeneity, resulting in highly variable responses to biologic therapies. Despite the efficacy of Infliximab (IFX), many patients fail to achieve sustained remission. Identifying biomarkers predictive of treatment response is essential for advancing precision medicine in UC. Gene expression profiling of colonic mucosal biopsies from IFX responders, IFX non-responders, and healthy controls was performed using a multiplex array, followed by technical confirmation by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemical assessment to further characterize tissue expression and biological relevance. IFX non-responders displayed a stromal–immune molecular signature marked by extracellular matrix remodeling, stromal remodeling, integrin-mediated signaling, and persistent inflammatory pathways. SPARCand SPP1emerged as the most prominent biomarkers, with significantly increased gene and protein expression in non-responder patients, highlighting their association with chronic tissue remodeling and therapeutic resistance. Mucosal resistance to IFX is associated with a specific stromal–immune profile characterized by SPARC and SPP1 upregulation. These findings suggest that both molecules may serve as promising candidate markers for patient stratification, highlighting the need for future prospective studies to explore their role in personalized management strategies for ulcerative colitis.

Article.Title: Cynaroside Attenuates Ethinylestradiol-Induced Cholestatic Liver Injury by Modulating the FXR/BSEP/CYP7A1/SHP Axis
Article.Authors: Hamed A.; Al-Nouri D.; Mahrous N.; Bassit A.; Abouelella A.; Hassan A.; Mokhtar G.; Ahmad G.; Osman A.; Ahmed A.; Mahgoob A.; Thabet S.; Abdel-Latif H.; Shamlan G.; Zhao H.; Al-Farga A.; Soliman S.
Article.Abstract: Cholestatic liver diseases are characterized by disrupted bile acid homeostasis, oxidative stress, and inflammation, ultimately leading to progressive hepatic injury. Although ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) remains the standard pharmacological therapy, its therapeutic efficacy is limited in several cholestatic conditions. This study investigated the hepatoprotective effects of cynaroside (CYN), a naturally occurring flavonoid glycoside, against ethinylestradiol (EE)-induced cholestatic liver injury and explored its underlying molecular mechanisms. Female Wistar rats were randomly allocated into four groups (n = 7): control, EE, EE + CYN, and EE + UDCA. Liver function indices, bile acids, cholesterol, oxidative stress and inflammatory biomarkers, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, Western blotting, qRT-PCR, and molecular docking analyses were performed. EE administration induced pronounced cholestatic liver injury, as evidenced by impaired liver function, hepatic accumulation of bile acids and cholesterol, oxidative imbalance, inflammatory responses, and marked histopathological alterations. CYN significantly ameliorated these biochemical and histological abnormalities, reduced hepatic bile acid and cholesterol accumulation, restored redox homeostasis, and attenuated inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, CYN modulated the hepatic FXR/BSEP/CYP7A1/SHP regulatory network, modulated hepatic FXR and Nrf2 protein expression, suppressed NF-κB activation, and favorably regulated TNF-α, IL-1β, and BCL2 expression. Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings further confirmed substantial preservation of hepatic architecture following CYN treatment. Molecular docking revealed favorable interaction of CYN with the FXR ligand-binding domain, with a predicted binding free energy of −8.18 kcal/mol, comparable to that of UDCA (−7.95 kcal/mol). Cynaroside attenuated EE-induced cholestatic liver injury by improving bile acid homeostasis and mitigating oxidative and inflammatory responses, potentially by modulating FXR-associated signaling and its downstream regulatory network. Collectively, the results provide a rationale for continued investigation of cynaroside in the context of cholestatic liver injury.

Article.Title: Conformational Sampling of CPT1A Enables Dynamic Structure-Based Ligand Screening
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Zhang Y.; Zhao J.; Long J.; Zhang L.; Yang Z.
Article.Abstract: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) catalyzes a rate-limiting step in fatty acid β-oxidation and is a target for studies of metabolic disease and cancer. However, the structural dynamics of CPT1A remain poorly understood due to the lack of full-length structure. In this study, we employed an integrated computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Markov state models (MSMs), and binding free energy calculations to elucidate the conformational landscape of human CPT1A. We performed an all-atom MD simulation of CPT1A embedded in a realistic outer mitochondrial membrane, and root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF)-guided local region analysis coupled with MSM transition-path analysis and GROMOS clustering convergently identified a representative conformation. The pathway probabilities reported here describe dominant local transitions within specific mobile segments rather than the global equilibrium population of the full-length protein. Using this representative conformation, we performed a virtual screening of over 1.23 million compounds from the ChemDiv library, followed by Lipinski filtering, yielding five candidates with docking scores below −10 kcal/mol. Subsequent MD simulations and binding free energy calculations confirmed stable binding, with compound 2 exhibiting the most favorable free energy of −25.99 kcal/mol. Principal component analysis (PCA) and secondary-structure analyses revealed ligand-specific modulation of CPT1A dynamics. A preliminary in vitro CPT1 activity assay revealed candidate-specific responses, and the free-energy and activity data were partially consistent. These results provide a dynamically informed structural basis for CPT1A ligand recognition, identify candidates with distinct energetic and functional profiles, and establish an integrated strategy for ligand discovery in structurally uncharacterized proteins.

Article.Title: Recycled PET/Sepiolite Composite Adsorbent for Methylene Blue Removal: Formulation, RSM Optimisation, Reusability, and Adsorption Mechanism
Article.Authors: Mohd Din S.; Khan Z.; Mohsin M.; Mousa S.; Othman N.; Younes M.; Mohamad Z.; Hossain S.
Article.Abstract: This study explores the valorisation of post-industrial recycled polyethylene terephthalate (rPET) via incorporation of sepiolite clay to develop a composite adsorbent for methylene blue (MB) dye removal. The composite formulation was evaluated by varying the rPET concentration, TFA:DCM solvent ratio, sepiolite content, and blending time. The selected formulation had an average particle size of 267.10 nm, a specific surface area of 0.67 m2/g, and a pore volume of 0.003925 cm3/g. Adsorption conditions were then optimised using a five-factor, three-level Box–Behnken design, considering contact time, MB concentration, adsorbent dosage, pH, and temperature. The resulting quadratic model was statistically significant (F = 114.18, p < 0.0001), with R2 = 0.9892, adjusted R2 = 0.9805, and predicted R2 = 0.9568; however, the lack-of-fit was also significant (F = 90.90, p < 0.0001), indicating that model predictions should be interpreted within the investigated factor ranges. At the selected conditions of 62.5 min, 25.5 mg/L MB, 2.55 g/50 mL adsorbent, pH 7, and 55 °C, the model predicted an MB removal efficiency of 99.03%. The adsorbent retained at least 93% reusability efficiency after six adsorption–washing–reuse cycles. The kinetic data were described more closely by the pseudo-second-order model, whereas the Freundlich model provided a better representation of the equilibrium data (R2 = 0.9976). Thermodynamic results indicated that adsorption was favourable and exothermic within the investigated temperature range. Overall, the results show that post-industrial PET can be converted into a value-added sepiolite-containing adsorbent for MB removal.

Article.Title: Biofluid Biomarkers of Neuronal and Glial Injury in Epilepsy and Seizures: A Comprehensive Review
Article.Authors: Moroșanu V.; Maier S.; Roman-Filip I.; Moroșanu S.; Bălașa R.
Article.Abstract: Epilepsy is one of the most common chronic neurological disorders worldwide, affecting millions of individuals and imposing a substantial cognitive, psychological, social, and economic burden. Despite significant advances in epilepsy research, key questions remain unresolved regarding the mechanisms underlying drug resistance, cognitive impairment, depression, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, as well as the contribution of recurrent seizures in promoting neuronal and glial injury. Addressing these challenges requires reliable biomarkers capable of accurately reflecting disease activity and detecting ongoing brain damage. In this review, we summarize the current evidence on biofluid biomarkers of neuronal and glial damage in epilepsy and seizures and discuss their potential clinical relevance. Particular attention is given to biomarkers associated with major pathways involved in epileptogenesis, including neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, neurodegeneration, blood–brain barrier disruption, altered gene expression, and synaptic remodeling. Emerging evidence suggests that circulating and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers may provide valuable insights into seizure-related brain injury and the molecular mechanisms underlying epilepsy. Although none of these markers has yet been adopted in routine clinical practice, they represent promising tools for improving diagnosis, prognostic assessment, patient stratification, and the development of more personalized therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Exploring the Role of Umbilical Cord Blood Leptin and Visfatin in Fetal Growth: Associations with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus and Neonatal Anthropometric Measurements
Article.Authors: Styliou M.; Tiptiri-Kourpeti A.; Konstantaras P.; Tsikouras P.; Nalbanti T.; Kritsotaki N.; Gerente A.; Nikolettos K.; Nikolettos N.
Article.Abstract: Leptin and visfatin are adipokines involved in metabolic regulation and fetal development, but their associations with maternal gestational diabetes mellitus and neonatal growth remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the relationships between umbilical cord blood leptin and visfatin concentrations, maternal GDM status, and neonatal anthropometric characteristics. Umbilical cord blood samples from 88 neonates were analyzed for leptin and visfatin concentrations using ELISA. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics v.32. Cord blood leptin concentration was significantly higher in neonates born to mothers with GDM than in those born to mothers without GDM (median [IQR]: 2.22 [1.09] vs. 1.50 [0.77] ng/mL; p = 0.002). Visfatin concentration was positively correlated with birth weight (r = 0.359, p < 0.01) and head circumference (r = 0.233, p = 0.029), and differed significantly across neonatal weight categories (p < 0.001). Post hoc analysis showed significant differences in visfatin concentrations between AGA and LGA neonates (adjusted p < 0.001) and between SGA and LGA neonates (adjusted p = 0.008). In multivariable regression analysis, the models explained 9.3% and 20.5% of the variability in leptin and visfatin concentrations, respectively. Umbilical cord blood leptin and visfatin concentrations were differentially associated with maternal metabolic status and neonatal growth characteristics. GDM status was independently associated with cord blood leptin concentration, whereas neonatal weight category was independently associated with visfatin concentration. These findings suggest that cord blood adipokine concentrations may reflect aspects of the intrauterine metabolic environment and fetal growth; however, their clinical significance and potential predictive value require confirmation in larger longitudinal studies.

Article.Title: Circular RNAs in Skeletal Muscle Aging and Sarcopenia: Mechanistic Evidence, Biomarker Potential, and Therapeutic Readiness
Article.Authors: Ngo T.; Lee W.
Article.Abstract: Skeletal muscle aging arises from interacting defects in proteostasis, mitochondrial quality control, inflammatory signaling, neuromuscular integrity, regenerative capacity, and mechanical–metabolic plasticity, and may culminate in sarcopenia. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are plausible regulators and biomarker candidates, but most evidence derives from developmental myogenesis, expression profiling, or non-aging atrophy models. This critical review organizes the literature around skeletal muscle aging and applies a four-level framework encompassing discovery, mechanistic support, in vivo causality, and functional intervention. We assess human linkage, species, treatment timing, locus of action, and endogenous or engineered modality separately. circSnd1 and circDdb1 currently provide the strongest combination of functional preclinical evidence and association with aged human skeletal muscle. circFUT10, circBBS9, circNEB, and circGLIS3 define less mature regenerative, discovery, histological, or muscle-quality domains. Non-aging atrophy studies, including circTmeff1 and engineered circmiR-29b, test whether proposed mechanisms remain active under defined catabolic stress. Human blood and serum-vesicle studies provide discovery-level associations with strength or mobility, but clinical validation of a circulating circRNA biomarker for sarcopenia remains insufficient. Therapeutic development is constrained by quantitative target credibility, systemic skeletal-muscle exposure, post-onset functional efficacy in aged organisms, safety, reversibility, and independent replication. The field should now prioritize rigorous validation over additional descriptive cataloging.

Article.Title: The First Report of a Bang-Sensitive Strain in Drosophila funebris: Molecular-Genetic and Lipidomic Characterization
Article.Authors: Kosherova K.; Abashkin D.; Zakharzhevskaya N.; Kazakova V.; Vorobyeva E.; Symonenko A.; Mukha D.
Article.Abstract: Bang sensitivity (BS) is a well-characterized seizure-and-paralysis phenotype in Drosophila melanogaster, but its genetic basis remains unexamined in the phylogenetically distant sister species Drosophila funebris. Here, we identify a naturally occurring BS strain in D. funebris from a wild population near Lake Valday, characterized by acute mechanical shock-induced seizures and paralysis, and examine its molecular-genetic and lipidomic basis. Comparative transcriptomics identified 241 differentially expressed genes (FDR-adjusted p < 0.05), with “fatty acid metabolic process” as the most enriched GO term. Notably, within this pathway, the peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase gene Acox57D-d showed the most significant downregulation (log2FC = −4.21, padj = 4.1 × 10−110), validated by head-specific RT-qPCR. Untargeted lipidomics of BS heads (LC-Q-TOF-MS) revealed 145 altered lipid species, dominated by oxygenated triacylglycerol accumulation, cardiolipin/phosphatidylethanolamine depletion, and a divergent shift—depletion of DG 29:0 and accumulation of DG 47:4, reflecting impaired peroxisomal β-oxidation and potential mitochondrial and Na+/K+-ATPase dysfunction. These findings nominate Acox57D-d as a leading candidate gene associated with the phenotype and molecular signature of the studied BS line and establish this natural BS strain as a potentially useful model for investigating the relationship between peroxisomal lipid metabolism, neuronal excitability, and insect thanatosis.

Article.Title: Folate Deficiency Drives Metabolic Dysfunction, Oxidative Stress, and Inflammation in HK-2 Renal Tubular Cells
Article.Authors: Chiu T.; Liu H.; Lin B.
Article.Abstract: The growing aging population has been accompanied by an increasing prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD), highlighting the need to better understand modifiable dietary and metabolic factors that contribute to renal injury. Folate deficiency and excessive fructose intake have been implicated in renal inflammation; however, the underlying cellular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of folate deficiency or fructose exposure on inflammatory responses, lactate metabolism, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial function in human renal tubular epithelial HK-2 cells. Folate deficiency markedly increased the secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokines interleukin-6 (IL-6) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), accompanied by enhanced NF-κB activation, both in the presence and absence of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation. Notably, folate-deficient cells exhibited increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity, intracellular lactate accumulation, and lactate secretion. Exogenous lactate supplementation or modulation of lactate production using the LDH inhibitor oxamate further demonstrated that elevated lactate promoted IL-6 and transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) production, NF-κB activation, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Consistent with these findings, folate deficiency significantly reduced the oxygen consumption ratio (OCR), indicating impaired mitochondrial function and a metabolic shift away from oxidative phosphorylation toward increased lactate production. High fructose exposure also enhanced IL-6 and MCP-1 secretion, particularly following LPS stimulation, while both LPS exposure and folate deficiency further increased lactate production. Collectively, these findings identify lactate accumulation as a potential metabolic link between folate deficiency, inflammation, oxidative stress and fibrotic signaling in renal tubular HK-2 cells. This metabolic-inflammatory pathway may contribute to the initiation and progression of CKD and highlights folate status and lactate metabolism as potential targets for preventing diet-associated renal injury.

Article.Title: Special Issue “The Role of Toll-like Receptors (TLRs) in Infection and Inflammation: Third Edition”
Article.Authors: Kircheis R.; Planz O.
Article.Abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are central players of the host innate immune system, functioning as germline-encoded pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) that monitor extracellular and endosomal environments [...]

Article.Title: Red Blood Cells Beyond Oxygen Transport: Dynamic Regulators, Disease Biomarkers and Therapeutic Platforms—A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Vives-Corrons J.
Article.Abstract: Red blood cells (RBCs) have traditionally been regarded as passive carriers of respiratory gases. Increasing evidence, however, indicates that they are active participants in vascular homeostasis and respond to mechanical, metabolic, and oxidative stimuli. This narrative review examines the interconnected roles of RBCs as regulators of vascular physiology, indicators of hereditary and systemic disease, therapeutic targets, and delivery platforms. RBC deformability, membrane organization, ion-water balance, metabolism, and redox capacity support microcirculatory flow, while ATP release, nitric oxide handling, adhesion, and extracellular-vesicle formation influence vascular function. RBC morphology, mechanics, hydration, metabolism, oxidative status, and vesiculation can provide clinically relevant information, although emerging functional and molecular biomarkers require further standardization and validation. RBC-directed treatments and RBC-based carriers offer additional therapeutic opportunities. Automated image analysis and machine-learning-assisted microfluidic classification are the most substantiated artificial-intelligence applications; broader multimodal decision-support systems remain exploratory.

Article.Title: Downregulation of GJA1-Derived circ_753 and circ_755 Differentially Modulates miR-182-5p Expression and Breast Cancer-Associated Phenotypes
Article.Authors: Maatouk N.; Briand J.; Ismael J.; Andraos S.; Kurdi A.; Lelièvre S.; Nasr R.; Talhouk R.
Article.Abstract: CircRNAs are key regulators of gene expression. The functional roles of exonic versus exon–intron circRNAs in early breast cancer remain unclear. Connexin-43 (GJA1) generates exonic circRNA (ecircRNA) hsa_circ_0077755 (circ_755) and exon–intron circRNA (EIcircRNA), hsa_circ_0077753 (circ_753), both linked to increased breast cancer risk. We examined their structural, molecular, and phenotypic roles in transient and stable knockdown S1 breast epithelial cells, using RT-qPCR, dual-luciferase, lumen formation and invasion assays, and extracellular vesicle (EV) analysis. Knockdown of cytoplasm-enriched circ_755 reduced Connexin-43 transcript and protein, whereas knockdown of nuclear-enriched circ_753 preserved GJA1. Both induced lumen disruption, β-catenin disorganization, increased invasion, and regulated onco-miR-182. More pronounced miR-182 upregulation and broader repression of tumor-suppressive targets (BCL2, FOXO1, RECK) were observed in circ_753 knockdown cells, alongside concurrent depletion of hsa_circ_0008932 (circ_8932), which is predicted to interact with miR-182. Similar reciprocal changes in circRNA/miR-182 were observed in released EVs. These data highlight circRNA-miR-182 networks with distinct effects on tumor initiation and potential value as breast cancer biomarkers.

Article.Title: Extraction, Structure–Activity Relationships, and Modification of Plant-Derived Polysaccharides: An Integrated Framework for Evidence-Based Method Selection and Bioactivity Optimization—A Review
Article.Authors: He Y.; Xin Y.; Zhang X.; Han D.; Liang Q.; Kong L.; Guan Y.; Sun H.; Liu C.; Han Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Extensive research has been conducted on plant-derived polysaccharides, yet three interrelated challenges remain insufficiently explored: extraction methods are often selected without systematic validation; the structure–activity relationship (SAR) remains fragmented; and modification strategies are rarely designed on the basis of SAR knowledge. This article systematically summarizes three key aspects: extraction, SAR, and structural modification. We critically compare various extraction techniques and clarify that method selection requires consideration of source characteristics and application orientation. We also demonstrate that extraction conditions may affect structural integrity and, consequently, influence biological activity. Subsequently, we analyze SAR by examining molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, uronic acid content, and chain conformation to identify structural determinants of biological functions. Finally, we review chemical modification strategies and illustrate how their efficacy depends on structural features initially determined by extraction. By integrating evidence from these three stages, this review offers a practical framework to support rational, evidence-based development of plant-derived polysaccharides for applications in medicine, food, and biomaterials.

Article.Title: Expanding the Clinical and Molecular Spectrum of Cartilage-Hair Hypoplasia in the Mexican Population
Article.Authors: Robles-Espinoza K.; Esparza-García E.; Corona-Rivera J.; Pérez-Coria M.; Rodríguez-Gutiérrez P.; González García J.; Magaña-Torres M.
Article.Abstract: Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (CHH) is a rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia caused by variants in RMRP (RNA component of mitochondrial RNA processing endoribonuclease), which encodes a non-coding RNA. Despite its well-established clinical and molecular spectrum in some populations, data from Mexico remain limited. We report eight patients from seven unrelated families with CHH. Clinical and radiographic findings were assessed, and RMRP was analyzed by polymerase chain reaction and Sanger sequencing. All patients exhibited disproportionate short stature; prenatal long-bone shortening and short stature at birth occurred in 50%. Radiographs showed widened long bones and metaphyseal dysplasia in all patients. Extraskeletal manifestations were observed in four patients, each with a distinct feature: immunodeficiency, anemia, Hirschsprung disease, or lymphopenia. RMRP variants were identified in all patients, comprising two homozygous and six compound heterozygous genotypes. Eight variants were detected: three pathogenic (n.6C>T, n.147G>A, and n.72A>G), two likely pathogenic (n.127C>T and n.125C>T), two variants of uncertain significance (n.128G>C and n.215C>T), and a novel promoter deletion (n.-39_-19del) encompassing the RMRP TATA box, classified as likely pathogenic according to the ClinGen RMRP variant interpretation specifications (GN088, Version 1.3). This study expands the clinical and molecular spectrum of CHH in the Mexican population and provides additional evidence for RMRP variant interpretation.

Article.Title: Minor Myeloid Leukemic Populations in Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: A Potentially Underrecognized Mixed-Phenotype Tumor?
Article.Authors: Semchenkova A.; Lavrova P.; Kozeev V.; Demina I.; Mikhailova E.; Roumiantseva J.; Lagoyko S.; Kazakova A.; Novichkova G.; Karachunskiy A.; Zerkalenkova E.; Popov A.
Article.Abstract: In “bilineal” mixed-phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL), the proportions of lymphoid and myeloid leukemic cells may differ substantially. A myeloid component may constitute <10% of bone marrow (BM) cells and show subtle immunophenotypic abnormalities detectable by multicolor flow cytometry (MFC). The significance of minor myeloid leukemic populations in otherwise acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), including their association with lineage switch, remains uncertain. We retrospectively reviewed diagnostic MFC data from 5094 children with B-cell precursor or T-cell ALL. An additional minor myeloid leukemic population (<10% of BM) was identified in 92 ALL cases (1.8%), with a median of 3.0% of BM cells (0.2–9.2%). The frequency of ALL cases harboring a minor myeloid leukemic population was comparable to that of overt “bilineal” MPAL (with both populations ≥ 10% of BM cells), diagnosed during the same period. The myeloid populations expressed CD33, CD64, CD14, lysozyme, and markers shared with the dominant lymphoblastic population (CD19/CD7, CD34, CD117). Common genetic findings were high hyperdiploidy (n = 14), KMT2A rearrangements (n = 13), and BCR::ABL1 (n = 8). Although no expansion was documented in most patients, 6 of 83 newly diagnosed patients (7.2%) developed lineage switch to acute myeloid leukemia or overt “bilineal” MPAL. Most cases were managed successfully with standard ALL-directed therapy.

Article.Title: MoDeMol: A Decomposition-Based Evolutionary Framework for Multi-Objective Molecular Optimization
Article.Authors: Guo C.; Dai C.
Article.Abstract: Lead compound multi-objective optimization requires balancing mutually restrictive drug-like properties, yet conventional latent generative and evolutionary optimization methods suffer from structural-function misalignment, population structural redundancy and low search efficiency under limited evaluation budgets. This work proposes a decomposition-based evolutionary framework built on a score-informed latent space (MoDeMol), with four core innovations: (1) Contrastive fine-tuned Transformer-VAE latent space supervised by predicted dual-target activity scores to improve the alignment between latent spatial proximity and predicted target-activity profiles. (2) Hybrid population initialization combining lead latent perturbation and high-quality molecular bank screening to balance local scaffold retention and global high predicted-activity region exploration. (3) Adaptive resource allocation mechanism for dynamic subproblem computation scheduling to boost optimization efficiency when the property evaluation budget is limited. (4) Dynamic Morgan fingerprint similarity penalization to suppress structural redundancy and maintain diverse molecular scaffolds in the population. Extensive benchmarks on single-target GSK3β and dual-target GSK3β/JNK3 kinase optimization tasks demonstrate that MoDeMol outperforms MolFinder, JANUS and MOMO in success rate, Pareto hypervolume and qualified molecular yield. Quantitative latent-space analyses, qualitative visualization, scaffold tracking, and ablation experiments provide complementary evidence for the contributions of the proposed components. The proposed framework addresses representation alignment, structural redundancy, and search-resource allocation within a computational multi-target lead-optimization workflow under limited evaluation budgets.

Article.Title: Artificial Intelligence for Plant Gene Regulatory Networks
Article.Authors: Yu H.
Article.Abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are the maps that plant biologists most want to draw, with arrows pointing from transcription factors to the genes they control, explaining how plants develop and respond to the environment. Since experimental validation of even one arrow can take years, and a single plant genome harbours tens of millions of candidate TF–target pairs, this gap has driven the development of numerous computational methods for GRN inference. Here I review three generations of computational approaches to plant GRN inference and measure them against a five-level ladder of evidence, including statistical association, conditional dependence, physical binding, functional regulation and causal circuits. Classical statistics and machine learning have simplified complex gene expression data into clear, prioritised predictions. Techniques like single-cell and multi-omics methods help uncover cell type-specific networks based on chromatin accessibility and binding motifs. Now, deep learning can interpret cis-regulatory grammar directly from genome sequences, and foundation models trained on plant genomes and millions of cells hold exciting potential to share regulatory insights across different species. The most promising route forward is a lab-in-the-loop division of labour in which foundation models serve not as oracles but as hypothesis engines, collapsing fifty million candidate TF–target pairs into the few hundred edges most worth the bench’s time, with each round of validation sharpening the next round of prediction.

Article.Title: Combined Effects of Chlamydia pneumoniae Infection and Hypoxia on Glial Metabolism and Alzheimer’s Disease-Related Pathways
Article.Authors: Kuikel K.; McEwen A.; Mathiske T.; Wojtaszak L.; St John J.; Delbaz A.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease involves complex interactions among neuroinflammation and metabolic dysfunction. Emerging evidence implicates microbial pathogens and hypoxia as converging stressors, yet their combined impact on glial function remains poorly understood. Human astrocyte and microglial cell lines were exposed to four experimental conditions: (i) normoxic control, (ii) Chlamydia pneumoniae infection under normoxia, (iii) hypoxia control and (iv) Chlamydia pneumoniae infection under hypoxic conditions. Hypoxia was induced at 3% oxygen for 72 h. Cellular responses were assessed using NanoString nCounter transcriptomics using the Alzheimer’s Disease and Metabolic Pathways panels, Tandem Mass Tag proteomics, MTT reduction, glucose uptake, intracellular ATP quantification and amyloid beta quantification by ELISA. Combined exposure to infection and hypoxia was associated with cell-type-specific alterations in glial metabolic and transcriptional responses. Factorial transcriptomic analysis identified significant infection × oxygen interactions across both NanoString panels and glial cell types. Proteomic responses differed according to cell type and oxygen availability. Aβ40 and Aβ42 measurements demonstrated treatment-associated alterations in the extracellular Aβ peptide profile, including increased Aβ42/Aβ40 ratios following infection. Together, these findings demonstrate distinct and interacting effects of infection and hypoxia on glial metabolic and molecular responses and identify Alzheimer’s disease-related cellular changes warranting further investigation in physiologically relevant models.

Article.Title: Constant Light Versus Intermittent Constant Light/Recovery Regimen: Differential Effects on Pineal Ultrastructure, Clock Gene Protein Abundance, and Systemic Metabolism in Rats
Article.Authors: Anurkina A.; Kozlova M.; Chernikov V.; Gladyshev N.; Zavalishina L.; Kulbitskiy B.; Areshidze D.
Article.Abstract: Disruption of the natural light regimen is considered a key pathogenetic factor in the development of desynchronosis and associated diseases. The pineal gland, as a neuroendocrine organ, is a central component of the circadian system and the primary target of the pathogenic effects of disrupted lighting. However, it remains unclear whether the mechanisms of pineal damage differ between different types of light stress. In this study, 120 male Wistar rats underwent a comprehensive analysis of the morphofunctional state of the pineal gland under two lighting regimens: constant lighting and intermittent constant light. Using light and electron microscopy, immunohistochemistry, ELISA, and cosinor analysis, it was established that the two regimens induce qualitatively different types of light stress. The obtained data indicate that constant lighting induces a degenerative phenotype with loss of rhythmic organization, whereas the shift regimen produces a phenotype of chronic re-adaptation with hyperactivation of the lysosomal system, paradoxical overexpression of clock genes, and pronounced metabolic disturbances. The identified differential markers may serve as a basis for preclinical evaluation of the efficacy of chronobiotic therapy and for the development of prevention strategies for disorders associated with shift work and light pollution.

Article.Title: From Susceptibility Loci to Therapeutic Targets: The Genetic Architecture of IgA Nephropathy
Article.Authors: Dopierała M.; Nitz N.; Bursy J.; Garbowska A.; Dopierała W.; Schwermer K.; Pawlaczyk K.
Article.Abstract: IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and a leading cause of chronic kidney disease and kidney failure in young and middle-aged adults, characterized by considerable ethnic differences in incidence and prognosis. This review summarises the evidence that these differences are, at least in part, genetically determined and maps the identified susceptibility loci onto the pathogenic sequence of the disease. Worldwide prevalence gradient increases with eastward and northward distance from Africa, while showing the significance of ancestry rather than environment in diaspora populations. Familial clustering provides support for an inherited component, while methylation differences between monozygotic twins discordant for IgAN point to an additional epigenetic layer. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in Han Chinese, European, and Korean cohorts have identified susceptibility loci implicated in antigen presentation, mucosal and intestinal IgA immunity, complement regulation, and innate immune signaling. Mapping these loci onto the four-hit hypothesis shows that inherited variation acts at distinct, potentially separable nodes. The MHC region contributes approximately half of the SNP-based heritability, while the CFH/CFHR locus provides the strongest signal outside the MHC. The complement arm has become the principal therapeutic target because it is currently the most pharmacologically tractable. We conclude by reviewing mechanism-directed therapies together with the safety questions and patient-selection issues that accompany them.

Article.Title: Spatial and Epigenetic Polarity of the AR Promoter During Prostate Cancer Progression: An In Silico Analysis
Article.Authors: Krasnyi A.; Ivanov R.; Minskaia E.
Article.Abstract: The androgen receptor (AR) is a key regulator of prostate cancer progression, yet the relationship between AR promoter methylation, chromatin state, and receptor expression across distinct tumor phenotypes remains incompletely understood. We performed an integrative in silico analysis of the AR promoter region spanning −2000 to +500 bp relative to the transcription start site (TSS), combining motif predictions for 24 transcription factors (TFs) with DNA methylation, TF ChIP-seq, and histone modification profiles from normal prostate tissue, primary and metastatic tumors, and cell models. Integration of these datasets revealed pronounced spatial heterogeneity in the epigenetic organization of the AR promoter. The distal segment contained predicted motifs for the selected lineage-associated TFs FOXA1, GATA2, HOXB13, and NKX3-1 and showed substantial variability in DNA methylation. Reduced methylation at selected distal sites or regions was observed in primary adenocarcinoma and in AR-low and AR-negative tumors and cell models, including tumors with a neuroendocrine phenotype. In TCGA-PRAD primary tumors, between-sample differences in AR promoter methylation explained only a small proportion of the variation in AR mRNA levels. Within the distal FOXA1 motif cluster (−751 to −678 bp), within-sample-normalized FOXA1 signal was higher in primary tumors than in matched normal tissue and was further elevated in patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) originating from metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Exploratory analysis of matched normal–tumor pairs revealed a positive correlation between changes in distal FOXA1 signal and changes in proximal H3K27ac signal. AR-positive C4-2B cells retained proximal H3K27ac without detectable FOXA1 occupancy at the distal cluster, consistent with an alternative active promoter configuration. The proximal TSS-associated segment was generally hypomethylated but displayed heterogeneous chromatin states. The −280 to +100 bp region was a recurrent focus of H3K27ac enrichment. In VCaP cells, proximal AR and ERG ChIP-seq signals overlapped, although no AR motif meeting the screening threshold was detected in this region. H3K27me3 repressive mark profiles showed marked heterogeneity across the examined models and tissues. Among models used as normal controls, RWPE-1 and PrEC showed H3K27me3 enrichment around the AR TSS, whereas primary normal prostate tissue showed no comparable enrichment. Heterogeneity was also evident between AR-negative cell lines: PC-3 showed pronounced proximal H3K27me3 enrichment, whereas DU145 lacked comparable enrichment. The analyzed mCRPC metastases likewise did not exhibit a profile comparable to that of PC-3. In AR-negative PC-3 cells, the proximal region additionally showed enrichment of KDM2B, PCGF1, and RNF2, together with strong H2AK119ub1 enrichment.
